The composite is cached like any node output, and re-runs are free anyway. Layers or Sketchpad? Layers reconciles finished images (masks between versions, after the generation). The Sketchpad makes an image by hand to generate from (draw, place, arrange, before the generation).

Blend a scene with one or more reference images. Wire the base image into scene, the sources you want to pull from into reference, and a prompt describing the blend. Compose is handy for dropping entourage, materials or mood from references into a render. It is also the house tool for grade transfer: scene = your shot, reference = the image whose look you want, prompt = the built-in Grade match preset (in the Prompt node's Presets menu) — the palette, tones and mood carry over while the architecture stays untouched. This is the recommended finishing pass after a Multi-Shot exploration. The same pass can borrow the reference's camera too: the Grade & camera match preset asks for its "filmic point of view" as well, and the shot is reframed to the reference's way of seeing — angle, symmetry, distance — while the building stays yours. Field-proven on a daytime pool shot turned into a frontal mirror composition in one call.

Every model and its default parameters come from Brut's catalog, so the menu is always current. Cheapest-to-richest on Gemini: gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image (Nano Banana 2 Lite, ~$0.03, text-to-image only — it can't edit) → gemini-3.1-flash-image (Nano Banana 2) → gemini-3-pro-image (Nano Banana Pro, up to 4K). For edits, the legacy gemini-2.5-flash-image (Nano Banana, ~$0.04) is still the cheapest and stays on the edit menus. See Providers for the full list and billing notes.
→ Multi-Shot & boards — explore many viewpoints at once.

Compose before you generate. The Sketchpad is a simple painter on a fixed canvas: brush strokes, wired images placed as movable layers, generation layers that render your marks in place, one stack. It flattens locally, for free, into the raster the generators consume. Typical use: block massing or a silhouette over a site photo, place an object where it should go, scribble the shape of a change, then wire the result into Image→Image, Compose or Inpaint and let the model render what you drew.

images (in): any number of images. They do not flow through by themselves: they appear in the editor's tray, and you drop the ones you want in as layers. image (out): the flattened canvas as a PNG. (An earlier build also exposed a mask plug with the painted coverage; it is retired until a node can take a mask wire, and any wire saved from it is dropped when the graph opens.)

The first wired image sets the canvas size. With nothing wired, pick a preset on the node (1K or 2K in 1:1, 16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4). Once a sketch exists the size is locked; ✕ start over on the node clears the sketch and unlocks the choice. The canvas select (top of the right column) is what the flattened image shows wherever nothing covers it: white or black paper, or transparent for a PNG with alpha. With a wired photo as the bottom layer you never see it; erase a hole in that photo, or start from a blank canvas, and you do.

The tools sit in a rail on the left of the canvas, Photoshop-style; the bar above the canvas shows only the active tool's properties. Hover a tool for its shortcuts. The right column starts with the canvas select and the canvas size. Color works like Photoshop: a foreground / background pair in the properties bar (the brush paints the foreground; click the back square or press X to swap, D resets to black over white), an HSB panel at the top of the right column (the field is hue across and brightness down at the current saturation; H, S and B sliders with numbers), and a recent colors strip that fills with every color you paint or pick, kept per device. Brushes: six tips sit next to the color pair when the brush or eraser is active, each with a stroke preview. Hard round (the default, pressure drives the width), soft round, pencil (thin and grainy, a light touch stays faint), marker (a flat chisel that turns with the stroke: thin one way, wide the other, one width regardless of pressure), hard square and soft square. Picking a tip sets the softness slider and the two pressure boxes (size, opacity) to the tip's defaults; all three stay yours to override, so a soft round can drive opacity, or a pencil can keep one width. A mouse always paints at full pressure. The eraser uses the same tip. Your last pick is remembered on this device. Brush (B) and eraser (E) paint on paint layers. Size, softness and per-stroke opacity have sliders (while you drag one, the brush circle shows at the center of the canvas so you see the change), Alt + right-drag adjusts the brush like in Photoshop (horizontal = size, vertical = softness), with a Diameter / Hardness / Opacity readout beside the circles (solid = size, dashed = softness extent). With a mouse the cursor stays pinned; with a pen hold Alt, press the barrel button and drag (tip first then barrel, or barrel first, both work), the pen simply follows and the Windows press-and-hold ring is harmless, [ ] change the size, digit keys set opacity (5 = 50 %, 1 then 2 quickly = 12 %, 0 = 100 %). Pen pressure (Wacom & co) scales the stroke width; strokes are stamped, so the width follows the pressure smoothly through curves. After each stroke a small readout next to the pressure boxes says what arrived: pen · 78 % (pointer type and peak pressure) or mouse · no pressure. The second one means the tablet driver is sending mouse events, not pen events: enable Windows Ink for Brut in the tablet driver (Wacom: the app's Mapping tab) and pressure comes through. Shift+click draws a straight stroke from where the last stroke ended: click once for a dot, Shift+click elsewhere for the line. Eyedropper (I), or Alt held in any tool: press on the canvas to sample the composite, a swatch with the hex value rides the pointer, drag to hunt the exact pixel, release to pick it. Bucket fill (G): click a region to flood it with the current color at the stroke opacity. The tolerance slider widens what counts as the same color; sample all layers (default) reads the whole composite so you can fill inside the lines of a placed photo, unticked it reads the active layer alone. Transform (T, Ctrl+T, or V) shows handles on the selected layer: drag anywhere to move, drag a corner square to scale about the center (Shift+corner scales width and height independently), drag the stem handle above the top edge to rotate (Shift snaps to 15°). Works on paint layers too. Selections: the marquee (M) drags a rectangle, the ellipse (Shift+M cycles between the two) an ellipse, the lasso (L) a freehand shape. Shift at the start of a drag adds to the selection, Alt at the start subtracts, a plain drag replaces it, a plain click deselects. Pressed after the drag started, Shift constrains the marquee to a square or the ellipse to a circle and Alt grows the shape from the point you started at, like Photoshop. Ctrl+A selects everything, Ctrl+D nothing, Ctrl+Shift+I inverts. Ctrl+click a layer's thumbnail selects its painted pixels, like Photoshop (Ctrl+Shift+click adds them, Ctrl+Alt+click subtracts); Ctrl+click a mask chip selects the mask's white. Handy to recolor a shape: Ctrl+click the thumb, then Alt+Backspace. While a selection exists the brush, eraser and bucket only touch the inside. Ctrl+C copies the selected pixels of the active paint layer, Ctrl+X cuts them, Delete clears them, Ctrl+V pastes the copy as a new paint layer in place, with the Transform tool ready to move it. Selections live in the editor session only. Alt+Backspace fills with the foreground color, Ctrl+Backspace with the background color, like Photoshop: the active paint layer's pixels, or its mask when the mask chip is active (the color's grey level: white reveals, black hides). A selection confines the fill. One undo step. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo inside the editor (also the two arrows at the bottom of the rail): strokes, transforms, layer changes, background. The stack resets when you close the editor. Layers (right): the layer opacity slider at the top acts on the selected layer. Below it, the stack, top first, the only part of the column that scrolls. Eye toggles visibility, Alt+eye solos a layer (Alt+eye again restores what was shown), + (or Ctrl+Shift+N) adds an empty paint layer right above the active one (inside its group if it has one; on top when nothing is selected), ↑ ↓ reorder, 🗑 deletes (a group takes its children along). Drag a row to move it in the stack: the row lifts and a blue line shows where it will land; nothing moves until you release, and names never change. The 🗑 removes every selected layer. Double-click a name to rename it; right-click a row for a color label (Photoshop's eleven, shown as a colored edge, purely for organization) plus hide, rename and group. Layer masks, on paint layers, image layers and groups, exactly like Photoshop: the mask button in the tray (or the row menu) adds one, white = shows (Alt on the button adds a hide-all mask). The mask chip appears right of the layer thumbnail. Click the layer (name or thumbnail) to paint its pixels, click the chip to paint its mask; the active element carries the blue outline. Ctrl+I inverts the mask, Shift+click the chip disables it, Alt+click the chip views it white on black. While the mask is the target the color panel switches to greys (a black-to-white ramp, hue and saturation dimmed, brightness is the level, five grey swatches): white reveals, black hides, a grey reveals partially (so D then X flip between the two), the eraser hides, the bucket follows the same rule, and pressure, softness and selections apply as usual. With the mask active, the 🗑 deletes the mask and leaves the layer; select the layer itself to delete the layer. A group's mask applies to everything inside it as one. Masks move with their layer and are stored as files like paint layers; the row menu also offers reveal all, hide all, disable and remove. Groups: Ctrl+click rows to select several, Ctrl+G (or the folder button in the tray) folds them into a group (one level of folders, like a sketch needs), Ctrl+Shift+G dissolves the selected group. The folder row hides or shows its children as one, folds with the chevron, and moves as a block. Dragging a layer onto a group's child puts it in the group, dragging it onto a top-level layer takes it out. Groups are organization only: the flattened image is the same with or without them. Under the stack, the wired images tray: click one to add it as a layer (it lands fitted and centered; add it twice for two copies). Wheel zooms (past 1.5× the preview switches to full native resolution), middle-drag pans. ? (or the keyboard button at the bottom of the rail) shows the full shortcut table inside the editor. ✓ Use this sketch uploads the painted layers, flattens the stack and puts the result on the node: the image plug is live immediately. The node has no ▶ of its own: it is the door to the editor, and any run downstream re-uses the flatten for free until you edit again.

The one paid thing in the Sketchpad, and the reason the sketch exists: a generation layer turns your marks into a photoreal render, in place, without leaving the editor. Sketch the intent on a paint layer: where the thing goes, how big, roughly what shape, which colors. A forest, a sword, a piece of cloth can never be drawn in detail, and they do not have to be. Then press the ✦ button in the layer tray (next to +): with a paint layer selected it makes a generation layer that follows that layer; with anything else selected it makes a general one that follows every painted layer below it. (Also: Ctrl+Enter, or right-click a paint layer → ✦ Generate from this layer…) The new layer lands right above, its row shows ↳ and what it follows, and the properties bar becomes the layer's own, one row: ↳ follows: one paint layer, a previous generation (iterate on a take: "make the lake frozen" over the lake you just rendered, its visible region is the guide), all paint below, or whole scene below (rework): no marks at all, the flattened picture under the layer is the subject and the prompt changes it as a whole ("turn this image to winter, same character, same clothes"), generation layers included. A rework is always the whole frame, has no follow setting, and shows entirely (paint a mask if you want to keep parts of the original). Change the choice any time; the prompt: what the marks stand for ("a weathered oak bench", "a pine forest at low sun"); scope: whole frame / local. Whole frame sends the entire canvas and fits the take back to it. Local sends only the marks' region: their bounding box plus some room, extended to a clean aspect ratio (3:2, 16:9, and so on), never cropped into the marks. The model reworks that region at its size tier and the take is scaled back into place, up or down. This is how a 5000 px document stays a 5000 px document: nothing ever regenerates it whole, and you can edit it region by region at full production resolution. Canvases above 2048 px on the long side start in local; pick a size tier at or above the region's long side and the take lands without upscaling. The last region is drawn dashed on the canvas while the layer is selected, and the price dialog states its size and aspect before you pay; follow: loose / balanced / close, how strictly the marks bind. Balanced (the default) makes placement, size and extent binding and leaves the outline, materials and detail to the model. Close makes the silhouette follow the painted shape. Loose treats the marks as a suggestion of placement and size; the model bar: provider, image→image model (the default is GPT Image 2.5 Flare at high), size tier, quality, the ⇄ chip when the model runs through an aggregator, and the price of one render; ✦ Generate. The price is asked first, every time. Nothing renders on its own. The line under the canvas says where the layer stands. What the model sees is two pictures: everything below the layer flattened without the marks it follows (the photograph to edit), and the same scene with them, whole or cropped to the local region. The marks are the placement contract: the fixed instruction tells the model where the object goes, how big, roughly what shape and colors, at the strictness you chose; to match the scene's light, perspective, scale and grain; to cast the shadows and reflections it would really cast; to make every mark disappear; and to leave everything else exactly as it is. The render comes back whole-frame: the model may change what your object implies anywhere in the picture (a forest at low sun casts long shadows across the whole image). What you see of it is decided by the layer's mask, which is seeded from your marks: the sketched region plus some breathing room, feathered wide. So by default the untouched scene stays pixel-faithful, and you paint the mask white to reveal more of the take: the long shadow, the reflection on the floor, the disturbed sand. Reveal all if the model reworked the scene well as a whole. The mask never re-renders anything: the raster holds the whole frame, painting is free. The row menu offers Re-seed the mask from the sketch when you have redrawn the guide. Generate into a selection. Nothing needs to be drawn: make a selection (marquee, ellipse or lasso, or Ctrl+A) and press ✦ (or Ctrl+Enter). The new layer says ↳ into the selection: the selection becomes its mask (with a soft edge of a few pixels), the flattened scene below it is the model's only input, and the prompt says what goes there ("a red sports car", "a wet cobblestone patch"). The selection itself is consumed; the layer keeps its outline, which the region-outline button on the bar shows dashed on the canvas (off by default), and re-rolls, staleness and takes work as for any generation layer. Scope defaults to local: the region sent out is the selection plus some room, so the model works on what you selected; switch to whole frame when the prompt names the place itself. There is no follow dial: with no marks, placement is the selection. Drag an ellipse, press the spark, write what belongs there: the render lands inside the selection only **🕘 takes** on the bar lists every render this layer ever made, from the project ledger. **Use this take** brings any of them back as the layer's raster, fitted into the region it was rendered for, your mask kept, free; it shows as stale if the sketch or the prompt changed since. A re-roll is never destructive. The node face counts stale generation layers. The row says where the layer stands: not rendered, stale (the sketch below it, the prompt or the model changed since the take), done, rendering…, or failed with the provider's reason. A stale layer keeps showing its last take until you generate again; a take that still matches is free (Generate does nothing new). ↻ next to Generate asks for a fresh take of the same sketch and prompt, paying again. Every render is a normal generation on the ledger, with the layer named on the row. A rendered layer behaves like an image layer: eye, opacity, a mask you can paint, Transform. Its take is stored on the node the moment it lands, so closing the editor with Cancel never loses a paid render; ✓ Use this sketch flattens the stack with the generation layers in place. While a layer renders, its row carries the same travelling light as a running node on the canvas. Later: per-layer history and re-pin, and Generate-all-stale from ▶. A new Sketchpad opens with the first wired image already placed as the bottom layer and an empty paint layer selected, so you can draw right away.
Export PSD, for the old schoolers

Export PSD in the editor's footer, or right-click the node's preview → Export PSD…, writes a Photoshop file into the project's outputs/exports folder (no dialog; Explorer shows it). Every layer goes in, hidden ones included: paint, placed images and generation takes as raster layers at their placement (moves, scales and rotations baked), layer masks as Photoshop layer masks (feather and invert baked, since PSD has no such switches), groups as folders with their own masks, names, opacity, visibility and color labels. The merged image is the flatten you see on the node. Photoshop, Affinity, Krita and GIMP open it. The export is local and free; the file is written by Brut itself, no library in between.

Painting, layers and the flatten are local and free: no provider call, no ledger row. Only a generation layer's render is a paid call, always behind the price gate. Paint layers, masks and renders are stored as files in the project's outputs, so the graph stays small and a .brutpack or a NAS-rooted project carries the sketch along. Wired images enter as references to their file, not copies. If an upstream node regenerates, the layer keeps pointing at the file it was placed from; add the new image from the tray when you want it. Sketchpad or Layers? Sketchpad makes an image by hand (draw, place, arrange) to generate from. Layers reconciles finished images by painting clipping masks between versions. Use Sketchpad before the generation, Layers after it. Next: an importer for your own Photoshop .abr brush sets may follow.

Where Brut stops being a one-image-at-a-time tool. Multi-Shot explores a scene from many angles at once; the boards are the surfaces where you review, curate and route the results. Every board shares one review gesture: hover a tile and click its 🔍 to open the lightbox — the image fitted to your screen, wheel-zoom into the pixels, and ←/→ (or the on-screen arrows) paging through the whole board like a classical gallery. Clicking the image itself does nothing (no accidental tabs while panning the canvas); the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

A POV/composition explorer. Wire your base image(s) into a Multi-Shot node, pick an exploration scenario and a shot count, and a planner (Gemini, seeing all your base images) writes N distinct shot prompts. Then N image-to-image jobs fill a contact sheet on a resizable node — a worker pool runs several at a time. Scenarios ship as data — Editorial, Ballsy, Morning → Evening, Four Seasons, Dutch Masters, and a custom scenario that takes its brief from the node's Notes field. (Older climate scenarios — Cold North, Mediterranean, Desert — are retired: their weather registers now live as V2 deck cards. A saved graph that used one keeps working and shows it honestly as retired.) Notes live on the node — a text box right under the scenario picker steers the planner on any scenario, and for custom it is the brief. Wired text (a Prompt or Refine node into the notes input) still works and both flow to the planner — wire when the text has a life of its own, type when it's a one-off. Pair custom with the Scenario maker Refine preset for a strong brief. 💾 Save as preset appears under non-empty notes — it saves the text as a prompt preset in the global library, loadable from any Prompt node in any project. Multi-Shot explores points of view — the look comes after. For grade/style transfer, don't feed a look reference into the exploration (a former reference inlet did exactly that and was retired: it pulled every composition toward the reference and made sheets repetitive). Instead, run the shots you keep through a Compose node: scene = the shot, reference = the look image, prompt = the built-in Grade match preset ("use the color grading of the second image…"). You pay once per keeper instead of per exploration, and 1-to-1 transfer is far stronger. Plan caching — the shot list is cached on its own hash, so stable prompts keep per-shot caches working. 🎲 rolls a new shot list. Per-tile controls — ↻ re-rolls one tile (only that tile re-pays), ✓ / ✗ mark keepers and misses, 🕘 re-pins a past result for that specific tile. Curation flows downstream — ✓ shots flow out the main port (or all non-✗ if none are ticked), taking effect on the next cached run. The contact sheet uses a tidy, deterministic column count from the shot count (≤4 → 2×2, ≤9 → 3-wide, else 4-wide), so it stays neat at any node size. The node's corner grip sets its width only: the height always follows the content — the Notes box (eight lines minimum, drag its own corner for more), the controls and the sheet's rows of squares — so the tiles are never squashed. The eye button beside New shot list folds the sheet away (the shots are kept, the node shrinks to its controls; the Shot Board is the place to review them large).

New Multi-Shot nodes plan with V2; a small V1/V2 rollout next to the title switches generations (existing graphs stay on V1, the original planner frozen for honest comparison). V2 exists because static briefs make models repeat their favorite gags across projects — the same prop, the same weather trick, job after job. It answers with four pieces: Grammar briefs. Each scenario's V2 brief describes categories of moves instead of listing example shots, tells the planner its examples are calibration rather than a menu, and carries a small banned list of motifs this studio has worn out. The lists are data (multishot.json) — extend them whenever a gag gets tired. The card deck. Every plan draws a hand of ingredients from the scenario's pools (a light register, a life event, a prop domain, …) and must weave them through the set. The hand is shown as chips on the node before you ever run — visible surprise — and the little 🎲 beside the chips redraws it without starting a run. Draws are deterministic, so caching stays honest. Pick your hand. Random is the default, but the ✎ beside the chips opens the picker: one row per pool, each set to random or a card of your choice. Pinned cards always ride the hand (shown as accent chips; wild cards are pickable at any dial level), the Surprise dial fills the remaining slots randomly, and 🎲 redraws only those. Pin everything — or pin on Classic, which draws nothing on its own — and the hand is fully yours. Picks belong to their scenario's deck, so switching scenario clears them. The Surprise dial. Classic (no cards — the calm grammar brief alone) · Fresh (the default hand) · Crazy (a bigger hand including each pool's wild cards, plus a push toward the never-published). Avoid recent motifs (off by default). Every V2 plan reports the distinctive ideas it used, and the engine remembers the last ~20 per scenario across all projects. Tick the box and the planner is told what the studio already did recently — the direct cure for "the same idea on every job". The memory ages out, so retired classics eventually return. V2 also makes the planner model selectable — the text model that writes the shot list (the node's Provider/Model picks stay the image model that renders them). The default is Gemini 3.7 Flash; different planners have different instincts, which is itself a variety lever, and models with a reasoning dial expose it here too. The planner's reply is a JSON shot list, and text models occasionally break it (a stray quote in a long shot string was the usual case). Brut asks Gemini and OpenAI planners for JSON mode (valid JSON at the token level) and, should a reply still not parse, retries the planning call once before failing loudly — the Activity panel notes the retry. Planning calls cost cents; nothing is rendered until the list parses.

The review surface for a Multi-Shot node. Wire the Multi-Shot shots output into a Shot Board and get a large captioned grid — the prompt under each image, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ proxied to the source. Each tile has its own output plug (shot-<i>) so you can route one chosen shot into Compose or Image→Video. The board re-emits the curated pool from its bottom port. Tiles show each shot at its real aspect (a 9:16 batch is a column of portrait frames, never a 4:3 crop); the Multi-Shot node's own compact sheet stays square thumbnails — the board is where you judge the actual frame.

Makes the crew's stills pool visible. Every image you wire in becomes a numbered tile — and the tile number is the global still number the cinema agents refer to, which kills the invisible wire-order problem. ↑ / ↓ reorder (the number is the contract, so reordering changes what a wire carries — WYSIWYG). ✕ hide a tile / ↺ restore it in place. Per-tile ref-<i> output plugs address one still by its board number. Free and local — it's just a lens on the images you already have.

The cinema planning nodes: they read your stills and pass a plan document (JSON on a text wire) toward Film Shots. Planning runs on the LLM you choose — Gemini, GPT or Claude — on your own key; on models with a reasoning dial (GPT-5.6, details; Claude Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8, details) a Reasoning select appears — deeper thinking for harder plans, billed as output tokens. For the end-to-end story, see the Cinema Sessions walkthrough. The chain is: stills → Director → Storyboard → Film Shots. (The original four-agent crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor — is legacy, kept at the bottom of this page.)
The Director — the whole crew in one node

One agent that holds the entire film in its head: it analyzes your stills, writes the concept, the look and the executable shot plan in a single call, and wires straight into the Storyboard. Because one model plans every shot with full awareness of all the others, the plan comes out varied by construction: an arc distributed across the shots (atmospheric hook, materials, reveal, hero frames, a pull-back ending), focal length, framing scale, camera height and movement changing shot to shot, and a hard cap on how often any still may be re-used. Its dials: a Brief (what film) and a Style (what look) from the same libraries the crew uses, the shot count and runtime, a People dial (none / subtle / lively), and an Audio switch that has every clip carry a one-line ambient sound note (folded into generation for video models that actually produce audio — a silent model never gets sound words). The plan it writes also carries a concept paragraph: the film's emotional tone, arc, lighting mood and pacing, readable and editable in 📖 Review like everything else. Advanced dials — locked production choices. The Advanced disclosure exposes six craft dials: Camera (RED digital / ARRI / Sony Venice / Blackmagic / IMAX / 35mm / 16mm film), Lenses (clean primes / anamorphic / vintage / long-lens compression), Lighting, Composition, Emphasis and Movement (contemplative → kinetic). Each pick is a fixed clause the Director must obey — it overrides any conflicting style language — and every dial defaults to Director's choice, which adds nothing. The vocabularies are data (cinema.json), so the studio can grow them. The proof sheet is always ONE image. 🎬 Proof renders the whole film as a single contact sheet at the price on the bar — after a targeted revise, the same button re-renders it (an unchanged plan replays from cache, free; ↻ New take forces a fresh render of the same plan, paying again). 🕘 opens every sheet the film ever rendered, from the project ledger, and 📌 pins one — a pinned sheet stays the film's validated sheet (and keyframe reference) through plan edits and new takes, until unpinned. The node's Setup, plan and Proof sheet sections all collapse to keep the card compact. Your own brief and style are wires, not notes. The node has two labeled text inlets — brief (optional) and style (optional) — made for a Prompt node (whose text is saveable as a preset, or refined through a Refine). A wired brief composes with the select: the canned entry sets the genre, your wire carries the project's specifics, and where they conflict the wire wins — the node says "⇄ wired in" under the select so the precedence is never invisible. For a fully custom film, set the select to None and let the wire direct alone. The Notes box is just notes: extra guidance, always honored, never secretly the brief. The proof sheet — see the whole film for cents. Below the plan, the Director offers 🎬 Proof: ONE image generation renders the entire film as a numbered contact sheet — every frame, one shared grade — from your stills and the plan's prompts (pick the image model, size and quality on the bar; cheap settings are fine, this is for your eyes). Judge it, then ✗ the frames that fail (the chips match the sheet's number badges) and hit ✎ Reinvent — one planning call rewrites only the rejected clips with genuinely new compositions; every kept clip is code-locked back verbatim, whatever the model returns. Re-render the sheet for cents and loop until the film reads right. The spend ladder is the point: ~1¢ of plan → ~6¢ of proof → keyframes → clips, and you never pay the next tier until the previous one convinced you. The validated sheet then directs the keyframes. When a Storyboard downstream generates an invented shot's keyframe, the Director's proof sheet rides along as a reference with a code-locked instruction: render that frame of the sheet at full resolution — its composition, light and grading — using the reference stills for the building's true geometry and materials. The sheet is part of the keyframe's cache identity, so re-rolling the sheet honestly invalidates unpinned keyframes: what you validated is what gets produced. (The film's style bible is also folded into every keyframe render, sheet or no sheet, so independently generated frames read as one film. The sheet itself is never cropped or reused as a frame — its resolution is for human eyes only.) It emits the exact same plan document as the legacy DoP chain, so everything downstream is identical: the Storyboard, keyframes, end frames, Film Shots, Review and Revise.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor

Legacy since 1.1.1. The Director plans measurably better films in one call than the four-agent chain (one model holding every shot in its head keeps a film varied; the chain's later agents were contractually barred from fixing a weak shot list). The crew nodes are therefore hidden from the node browser — but they remain fully functional: every saved graph that uses them keeps loading and running, Review/Revise included. New films should start from the Director (or the Cinema Director library template).
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Scenarist

Writes the treatment — the story and beat structure — from your stills. You pick a brief (or custom, where your notes are the brief). Its contract enforces one shot = one still, so grounding stays honest. It may also invent shots — compositions no still contains (detail close-ups, reveals, human presence, pull-back endings; the Cinematic Reel (flourish) brief leans into this). An invented shot names the stills that anchor it and carries a written keyframe prompt; Brut generates that missing frame from your stills on the Storyboard before any video runs, so the identity never drifts. Still reuse is disciplined by contract — a still may directly ground at most two shots, never back to back — and the "Invent every shot" switch goes all the way: stills become references only, every start frame generated.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Artistic Director

Sets the look: a style bible and per-shot art direction — palette, lighting, mood. Choose a style (or custom). It builds on the Scenarist's treatment. On invented shots it also styles the keyframe prompt (palette, light, lens character) — composing the frame is exactly its job.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › DoP (Director of Photography)
Turns the treatment into an executable shot plan — the camera language, motion, and which still grounds each shot, as a concrete list of clips with durations. This is the plan Film Shots executes.
The legacy crew — Scenarist, Artistic Director, DoP, Script Supervisor › Script Supervisor
The continuity pass: harmonizes speed, light and palette across all the clips so the sequence feels like one film, not a pile of clips. Grounding is code-locked so it can't drift off the stills.

Not an agent but the crew's review surface. The Storyboard turns the plan into an editable board of shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, dynamic position badges. It emits concrete image paths, so Film Shots downstream only needs the plan wire. ✕ mutes, it never deletes. A muted card stays on the board, greyed and badged muted, out of the film: its keyframes, pins and prompts are kept, the position badges renumber around it, and ↺ on the card (or ↺ N muted in the header) brings it back in place. Only a hand-added shot can be deleted for good (🗑, once muted). The same discipline as the Shot Board's ✗: a clip you cut is a clip you can still see. Still numbers heal themselves. The stills are numbered from 0, but a model that counts them sometimes counts from 1, and every reference in its plan lands one too high (the last one pointing past the board: "anchor still #15 isn't wired in, only 15 stills"). That signature is unambiguous, so Brut renumbers such a plan in code, at the agent that wrote it and again on the Storyboard against the wired stills, and says so in the Activity panel. Anything that isn't that exact pattern is left alone and still fails loudly on the card. Never a silent clamp. Invented shots arrive frameless with a 🎨 Generate keyframe button: an image-to-image render on the shot's anchor stills (identity clause appended, conformed to the film's aspect — cents, priced on the board next to the image-model picker). Keyframes cache on their prompt + anchors, ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins, 🕘 opens the card's history — every keyframe it ever generated, from the project ledger, any past take re-pinnable as the start frame for free — a wired image overrides, and the start selector can still ground the shot on a real still instead. An invented shot with no keyframe blocks that clip in Film Shots — it is never silently sent as text-to-video. The board also owns the film's aspect ratio: a dropdown (defaulting to the DoP's format) that conforms every keyframe and travels in the emitted plan. Changing it re-crops the kept raw renders for free — no regeneration. ▶ on the board batch-renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation (count, per-frame price, total); the per-card 🎨 stays for one-offs. Its companion ↻ New takes re-rolls every generated keyframe at once — fresh takes on the current model, each paying again, one itemized confirm — for a model switch or a general do-over; 📌 pinned, wired and grounded cards are kept, and old takes stay pinnable in each card's 🕘 history. A prompts on/off switch declutters the cards, and the whole pre-wired chain ships as the Cinema Crew library template (File ▾ → Browse library…). End frames, on demand. Each card's end selector is none · a still · 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right — same image box, own in-socket and out-plug, own tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame: rendered image-to-image from that start frame as image 1, with the reference stills that show what the move reveals as grounded context (never for composition), continuity + identity clauses appended, conformed to the film's aspect. The crew writes its prompt: an end-frame writer embedded in the Storyboard (borrowing the LLM and reasoning dial of the crew node on the plan wire) sees the start frame image, the clip's shot plan and the reference board, drafts the frozen final frame of that one move and picks the stills (at most three) that ground what lies outside the start frame; ✎ / 🎨 open a review — start frame beside the editable draft, ✎ re-drafts, the still picks as toggleable thumbnails, Generate renders — so nothing renders from a prompt you haven't read. ↻ re-rolls, 📌 pins (surviving prompt edits and a re-rolled start; otherwise a new start orphans its end), 🕘 = the end frame's history. ▶ on the board reviews every armed card in one modal after the start keyframes. An armed end frame still pending blocks its clip downstream; a video model without an end-frame input runs the clip from the start alone and the Film Shots table says so on that row. Every frame block is also a source: the plug on its image edge carries that frame — the start frame (keyframe, wired image or grounded still) or the end frame — and a pending frame delivers nothing; the labeled plug bar at the card's bottom carries the clip's final prompt (overrides and wired prompts applied; in on the left, out on the right), an invented shot's keyframe prompt and the validated end prompt, for reuse or refinement anywhere. Card images can be dragged straight onto the canvas to detach into a ready-filled Image In.
📖 Review — read it like a document, direct it like a director

The raw JSON on the node face is for the wire, not for you. Every crew node has a 📖 Review button that opens the document as a document: the title as a headline, the analysis as prose, the style bible as labeled sections, every shot a numbered card with its prompt, camera, duration and grounding badges. Two verbs live in that modal, with two costs: Edit — free. Every text field is editable in place. Save writes each field back into the same place in the document, so the structure the downstream chain depends on can never drift; it behaves exactly like hand-editing the node's text, just humane. Anchors are editable too. An invented shot's card shows its anchor stills (the 0-based still numbers its keyframe is built from) as a small list you can rewrite: 0, 3. The field knows how many stills the node is wired to and flags any number the board can't serve, so a stray anchor is a two-second fix instead of a re-plan. 💬 Comment → Revise — one planning call (cents, ledgered). Every section and shot card takes a margin note ("shot 4 slower", "the whole film should feel like dusk"), plus an overall-notes box. Revise with comments hands the agent its own document and your notes; it returns the same document revised — same shot ids, same structure, only what your notes require changed — and the comments clear once addressed. A revision that would break the document contract is rejected and your document stays untouched. Comments survive closing the modal, and the node's Review button shows how many are waiting. They compose: fix wording directly, comment the conceptual asks, revise — the revision starts from your edited text.

Agent output is editable text. Hand-edit a plan and your changes flow downstream while inputs are unchanged; change an input or roll again (🎲) and the agent regenerates over your edits — deliberately. The planner sees your stills (downscaled for the model's request cap; generation always gets full resolution) and returns strict JSON, whose analysis is surfaced in the Activity panel. Grounding is code, not prose. One clip animates one keyframe — a still of yours, or a frame generated from your stills; the DoP's still-index references are reconciled in code, invented shots are blocked until their keyframe exists, and an anti-shake stability clause is appended to every clip — so the plan you approve is the film you get.
→ Video — shoot the plan, review the clips, cut the sequence.
Where stills become motion. Brut treats video like the expensive thing it is — every clip is quoted and confirmed before a cent is spent.

Animate a single image into a clip. Wire an image into the node, pick a provider and model, set duration/resolution and (where supported) audio and an end frame, and run. Providers: Kling (REST and subscription), Google Veo, Gemini Omni, and Seedance — see Providers. Some models do text-to-video too. The node shows a cost estimate before you run, derived from Brut's data-driven pricing. Clip length follows the model: Kling and Veo offer a few fixed durations, Gemini Omni 3–10 s, Seedance 2.5 anything from 4 to 30 s (or smart, where the model picks). On models whose clip must keep the start frame's aspect ratio (Seedance 2.5), the aspect select disappears while a start frame is wired and the node says so; the request is sent the way the provider demands. With nothing on the image inlet the run is text-to-video and the aspect select is back, since that run takes a ratio of your choice. Running a finished node again replays its clip from cache, free. Want another take of the same shot? The title bar's ↻ re-roll generates a fresh one (billed again, at the same estimate); the previous clip stays in the node's 🕘 history, pinnable. When a video model runs through an aggregator route (the "⇄ runs via …" chip — e.g. Kling v3 on your OpenRouter key), the node shows only the knobs that route actually accepts: settings the aggregator doesn't carry (like the aspect-ratio select or the negative prompt on OpenRouter's Kling) disappear rather than fail the run. The clip's aspect still follows the start frame you wire in. Add the native key to get the full control set back.

Some models accept extra reference images alongside the start frame — a character, a product, a style plate — and keep them consistent in the clip. When the selected model supports them, the node grows a references inlet and its info line says so ("✓ takes reference images (up to N)"); models that don't say that too, so you never guess. A Reference Board plugs straight in — its numbered tiles (or the whole curated pool) wire onto the inlet. Current support: Seedance 2.5 (up to 30, addressed as @Image1… in the prompt), Gemini Omni Flash, Kling o1 / 3.0 Omni (subscription, up to 6), Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1 / 3.1 Fast (up to 3). Wiring references into a model that can't take them fails with a clear message — Brut never silently drops an image you wired.
Film Shots — the cinema batch executor

Film Shots takes a shot plan (from the Director / Storyboard) and shoots the whole sequence. Its defining feature is the cost guard: It prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, estimated cost — and shows an itemized confirmation before any spend. Cancel a line and the total updates. Tick boxes choose what gets sent. Every row has one, all ticked by default; untick a clip and it stays in the table, greyed, not sent, not priced, not in the output pool — generate three, judge them, then tick the rest. The Σ row's box ticks or unticks everything, and its N of M clips line always says what Generate would actually send. Ticks are saved with the graph (never in library recipes). Cached and pinned clips cost $0 and are never re-quoted. It fans out on a worker pool (staggered to respect provider rate limits), with the same per-clip semantics as Multi-Shot: cache / ↻ re-roll / ✓✗ verdicts / 📌 pins. An anti-shake stability clause is appended to every clip, and audio is an explicit AND-gate. An invented shot whose keyframe hasn't been generated on the Storyboard is a per-clip error — that clip is blocked (and counted in the confirm), never silently downgraded to text-to-video. The rest of the batch rolls normally. Nothing is generated until you confirm the total. That confirm no longer freezes the rest of a running graph — other branches keep working while it waits. Like Image → Video, a routed model (the "⇄ runs via …" chip) shows only the knobs its route accepts — the quote table and the clips both use exactly what will be sent, and the film's aspect rides each clip's start frame.

The review board for Film Shots — video tiles, ✓ / ✗ / ↻ per clip, and per-tile clip-<i> plugs to route one clip onward. The video equivalent of the Shot Board. Tiles show a still poster of each clip (in the clip's own aspect ratio) and stay feather-light — press ▶ on a tile to play it; one clip plays at a time, and 🔍 opens it full-screen — ←/→ screens the whole board clip by clip. The /row select goes up to 15, so a whole reel can sit in one row.

Wire your curated clips into a Sequence node and it assembles them into one mp4 with local ffmpeg — cuts or chained crossfades, scaled and padded to a common size. It's free, cached, and needs no ledger. ffmpeg ships as a static binary inside Brut (no system install). The film follows the first clip's orientation — a pool of vertical 9:16 clips assembles into a vertical reel, not a pillarboxed landscape frame. The Quality select sets the short side (1080p vertical = 1080 wide). Clip audio is kept. Clips with native sound (Veo, Seedance, Kling with audio on) carry it into the film; silent clips get exact-length silence so nothing drifts; crossfades fade the audio too. A pool with no sound anywhere produces a clean video-only file.
The video nodes are the back half of the Cinema Sessions: Storyboard → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview. Read that walkthrough to see them working together.

Upscalers grow an image to delivery resolution — the finishing step after you've generated and curated. They are paid nodes: the source image goes to the upscaling provider with your own key, and cost scales with output pixels, not input.

Wire one image in (from Image In, any generator, a Shot Board tile…), pick a model, run. The upscaled image flows out the bottom port like any other image — into a Preview, a Conform, or straight to disk via the ledger. Batch: wire several images (an Image In folder, a curated Shot Board pool) and each one upscales as its own job — two in parallel, with a per-image cache, so a re-run only pays for what changed and a partial failure retries just the failures. The estimate line sums the whole set, and each output's 🔍 compares against its input. Caching works as everywhere: unchanged input + unchanged dials = free replay; the 🕘 history lets you re-pin any past result. The node shows a live estimate — input size → output size, megapixels, and the approximate cost — before you spend anything.

The archviz default.

The 🔍 on the node's result opens straight into a full-screen before/after comparison of the input against the upscaled output: drag the divider to sweep between them (the input is shown at the same size, so you're comparing detail, not scale). The mouse wheel zooms — the fast display copy is shown until you zoom, then the original files load so you're judging real pixels — drag pans when zoomed in, double-click resets, Esc or a click outside closes. The same wheel-zoom works in every magnified preview across Brut.

Your favorite dial combinations can be saved as named upscaling presets — the 💾 button next to the preset select stores the current model + dials in Brut's global library (all projects, both dev and installed app). Picking a preset applies it; editing any dial detaches it (your params are always the truth); ✕ deletes it from the library.

The clip finisher: wire one clip in (a Clip Board tile, an Image → Video output, a whole Sequence), pick a provider and model, choose a scale — plain 2x / 4x or a standard target: → HD, → 4K, → 8K (the target sizes the clip's short side, so a portrait 9:16 reel "at 4K" comes out 2160 wide) — and run. The upscaled clip flows out — audio is kept. Two providers, same models: Topaz Labs (cloud) — bills credits per job, works anywhere. Topaz Video AI (local) — free: if you own the Topaz Video desktop app, Brut runs the upscale on your GPU. No key, no credits, no confirm dialog, and the clip never leaves your machine. See the provider page. Nothing bills without your OK — every cloud run opens an itemized confirmation with the credit estimate first (cached and pinned replays never ask; free local runs don't either). Topaz's own analysis is the billing truth: the lower bound of its quote is billed and lands in the ledger. Cloud jobs can take a while on real clips; they run engine-side, survive restarts, and reattach. Local jobs simply re-run if interrupted — nothing was billed. Output caps at 8K per side; cloud uploads at 500MB. Model When Proteus 4 the general-purpose default — upscale, denoise, sharpen in one pass Rhea natural-texture enhancement, higher scales Gaia CG rendered/CG clips — archviz animations, clean edges

Upscales are priced by output image area (and for video, × duration). Magnific's doc rates work out to roughly €0.025 per output megapixel with a €0.10 minimum — Brut shows this as an approximate $ figure before the run, and the ledger records the estimate from the actual output pixels after it. Rough feel: a 1080p still → 4K is ~€0.20; pushing a 640×480 crop to 16x lands near €2. As everywhere in Brut: your key, your bill, zero markup.
Small, local, free — the glue between generation steps.

Brings stills to one aspect ratio before generation, so a set of mixed-ratio renders becomes a clean, consistent batch (video models in particular want a single ratio). Choose a target aspect ratio and a method — crop or pad. Per-image ✂ crop editor: drag an aspect-locked rectangle to choose which part of each still survives the conform (the default is a center cut — architecture rarely sits dead-center). The crop is stored per image; the engine crops the original at full resolution. The stills sit on a resizable board: pick 2, 3, 4 or 5 per row from the n / row selector and drag the node's corner to size the tiles; many stills scroll inside the frame instead of stretching the node into a column. Each image gets its own output plug, so you can route conformed stills individually. Each row's 🔍 opens the lightbox on the conformed result — ←/→ pages the whole set, so you can flip through the batch and check every cut. Conform runs entirely on your machine (local PIL) — free, never metered.

Inspect any output at screen size. Wire an image or video into a Preview node and it shows inline on a resizable frame, live: whatever is plugged in appears the moment it exists — when you open a saved graph, when an upstream node finishes, when you pin a past take — with nothing to press. There is no ▶ on the node (nothing to run; it is a viewing surface, like Compare). The image inlet displays video too. Hover a tile and its 🔍 opens the lightbox — wheel-zoom, and ←/→ pages through everything on the node. When several images are shown, the ‹ › buttons on each tile reorder them. Preview is the "show me the result" node you'll drop at the end of most branches; the full-resolution files live in the project's output folder.

Two images, one verdict. Wire any two takes into the A and B inlets — a Gemini attempt against a GPT attempt, an original against an Annotate correction, yesterday's keeper against today's re-roll — and the node shows them side by side, live, without running anything. Hover it and the 🔍 opens the real thing: the before/after wipe slider, both layers sharing one zoom and pan, so you can drag the divider across a facade while zoomed into the brickwork. The slider labels pick up the source nodes' names, so it reads "Image → Image vs Annotate & Correct", not "before vs after". Compare is a viewing surface, not a processor — free, local, no output port and no ▶ (there is nothing to run; the tiles follow the wires live — route the winner onward from its source node). It's the generalization of the Upscale node's built-in input-vs-result compare: same slider, any two wires you choose.

Every take a node ever made, on the canvas. Projects grow hundreds of generations and the good one from Tuesday is somewhere in the outputs folder. Wire any generation node's output into the History board (the image inlet takes video nodes too) and the board fills with every take that node ever produced, newest first, straight from the project's generation ledger. Wire several nodes in and the board shows one group per node, in wire order, each headed by the node's name and id, its take count and what it has cost so far. That is the point of the board: it reads as "what is inside this branch", not as a flat pile. Tiles carry the model, the date, the cost and, where it applies, the shot number of a Multi-Shot take, the card of a Storyboard keyframe or the Director's proof sheet. The prompt sits under the caption and in the tooltip. Every tile shows the take at its own aspect: a 9:16 take is a tall tile, a 16:9 take a wide one, never a crop, so a node that changed format mid-way reads truthfully. A tile's 🔍 opens the Magnifier, and ←/→ page through that node's whole history. Video takes play in place: a still poster at rest, click ▶ to play (one tile at a time, so a board of forty clips stays light). 📌 pins on the source node. The pin is exactly the 🕘 re-pin: the take becomes the source node's active output on every run, free, until you unpin it there or here. A pinned tile wears the amber ring. Multi-Shot tiles pin their own shot, Storyboard tiles their own keyframe. The board itself has no output and never runs anything: pins act on the source, so keep the downstream wires on the source node and use the board to choose. Drag an image tile onto the canvas to detach it as a ready-filled Image Input, the same gesture as dragging any preview out of a node. Right-click a tile for Reveal in Explorer, Copy, Export. Filter by model when a node has run on several, pick the tiles per row, ↻ re-reads the ledger (it also refreshes on its own whenever a tracked node finishes a run). Wires through a composite card or a reroute dot resolve to the node that actually generated: the board always shows the generator's own history. Wire two generation nodes into a History board: every take, grouped per node, pin one Free, local, nothing leaves the machine: the ledger is a file in the project folder. The board shows the newest 200 takes per node.

A sticky note for the canvas — annotate your graph the way you'd annotate a whiteboard: intent for future-you, instructions for a teammate opening the project later, review remarks next to the branch they're about. Notes aren't nodes — they're placement tools, living in the rail's Organize section (with Stamp, Group and Composite). Click the rail's sticky-note icon and the note rides your cursor: click the canvas to place it at the default size, or click-and-drag to draw its size (Shift places several, Esc or right-click cancels). While you're placing, the nodes underneath freeze — you can drop a note on top of anything. Double-click to write, click elsewhere to finish. Notes support a light markdown: # heading, - bullet, **bold**, *italic*, `code`. Select a note for the toolbar: five sticky colors, four fonts (Sans / Display / Hand / Mono), text sizes from 11 to 256px, bold and italic, left / center / right alignment, plus resize handles. Display order is fixed so annotations always show: stamps over notes over nodes (selecting anything still brings it to the front). Notes have no ports and never execute — free, local, never sent to any provider as part of a run. Notes travel: they're saved in graphs, templates and composites, so a library template can ship its own usage notes. Tidy moves them with the graph — each note keeps its position relative to the node it sits next to. Marcel reads them. A note sitting next to a node is exactly the kind of intent he should see — ask him about the graph and the notes are part of his picture. He can write them too.

A frameless emoji mark — the quickest possible annotation. Click the rail's stamp icon, pick your emoji from the flyout, and it rides your cursor; click to drop it — on empty canvas or right on a node (Shift-click for a trail of them). Drop a ⭐ on the keeper, a 🚧 on the branch under construction, a 💩 on what it deserves. Select a stamp to swap the emoji, resize it by the grip in its corner (like a sticky), or delete it. Free, local, no ports.

Draw on the canvas — made for Wacom people (mouse works too). The rail's Pen icon (or the ring's Pen slice) enters draw mode: sketch freely, pen pressure sets the stroke weight, pick a color (theme ink + the five sticky colors) and a width, Alt-click erases a stroke, and Esc or ✓ finishes — the whole session lands as one frameless drawing you can move, resize (it scales as a unit) and delete like any annotation. Free, local, never sent anywhere.

A clean label — for those who prefer tidy organization over stickies: the same note machinery with the paper removed. No fill, no shadow, just typed words on the canvas — perfect for titling regions of a big graph. The label sizes to its content by default; select it and drag the knob on its left or right edge to set the width (the height always follows the text, so a title never clips; double-click a knob to fit the text again), and the font size is its scale control, up to a poster-sized 256px. It gets the full note toolbar (four fonts, sizes, bold, italic, alignment), and the colors apply to the text itself, with a theme-ink default.

Right-click any empty spot on the canvas and a radial menu opens under your hand — every organize tool one flick away. The center names the ring you're on and clicking it cycles three states: Organize (note · stamp · pen · text · group · composite · add node · tidy) → your most-used nodes (learned from your own placements) → your recent stamps. Nodes land where you right-clicked; the annotation tools (note, stamp, text) hop onto your cursor so you place — or click-drag-size — them exactly like from the rail. Power move: press the right button, drag onto a slice, release — picked, no clicking. The rail keeps every tool too; the ring is just the fast hand. That's the whole palette. Back to Nodes & graphs for how they run together, or on to the Providers.

Brut is bring-your-own-key. You add a key for each provider you want to use; the engine calls that provider directly, on your key, at their price. Brut never holds a key that bills anyone but you, and never marks up a token.

⚙ Settings on the left rail (or the setup wizard) shows every provider as a card — its role, and one status line — grouped by what it does (generation, aggregators, upscalers). Click a card to paste a key (validated on save); the switch on the card turns a provider off without deleting anything. Keys live in your OS keychain — never in a graph, never sent anywhere but the provider. You can also set them via environment variables before launching the engine.
The one rule that trips everyone up

Image and video models need a billing-enabled key. Free tiers usually have zero generation quota, so your very first call returns a 429 — that's billing not enabled, not throttling. Turn on billing in the provider's console and it clears.

Model routes — native first, aggregator fallback

Some models can also run through an aggregator — a third-party service (like an aggregator subscription or a multi-model API) that resells the same model under its own billing. Brut treats those as routes, with three hard rules: Your direct key always wins. If you hold the native provider's key, the generation goes straight to the provider, exactly as before. Routes only activate for a model when you have no native key but do hold the aggregator's credential. Routing is always visible. A routed model shows a ⇄ runs via … chip on the node, the run confirm says who bills, and the ledger records it. Nothing routes silently. The catalog stays curated. An aggregator credential never adds models to Brut — the model list is exactly the one Brut ships, whatever route serves it. Estimates for routed runs come from the route's own measured price, or are absent; aggregators typically charge a margin over the direct API, and the node says so. Availability is resolved once at engine start and re-resolved the moment you add or remove a key — adding an aggregator credential mid-session lights up the routed models immediately. Four route providers ship today: OpenRouter (one key for text + images with Brut's native menus + the whole video set — billed cost recorded per job), fal.ai (API key — Nano Banana family, GPT Image 2, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1), Higgsfield (subscription plan credits, browser sign-in — Nano Banana 2, Seedance 2.0) and Replicate (API token — Nano Banana Pro/2, GPT Image 2, Kling Omni, Veo 3.1 incl. end frames, Seedance incl. text→video). When several credentials exist, that same order decides. Text models route too: with an OpenRouter key (or, text-only, a fal.ai key) the planning models — Refine, the Multi-Shot planner, the cinema crew, Text→Text — run at pass-through token rates when no native text key exists. Marcel routes through OpenRouter too — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through (verified live), so one OpenRouter key is a complete text seat. Deciding between direct keys and an aggregator? The full pros/cons and a feature-by-feature capability matrix live on Keys vs aggregators.

Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic double as planning models — they power the Refine node and the cinema crew, where you pick which LLM writes your treatment or shot plan. Text models never enter the paid generation queue; they're cheap and separate. Provider errors (4xx/429) are surfaced verbatim on the node — Brut never masks them, so what the provider says is what you see.

Brut is bring-your-own-key at heart: the cheapest, highest-fidelity way to run it is a handful of native provider keys, and nothing Brut does ever adds a markup to them. But not everyone wants to open four provider consoles — so Brut also speaks to aggregators, as routes: your aggregator credential serves models you have no native key for, visibly, at the aggregator's own prices. Three setups cover almost everyone. Pick by what you care about most:
Which path should you pick? › 1. Native keys — pick this if you care about price and control

Gemini + OpenAI + one video provider (+ Anthropic for Marcel's best brain). This is what Brut is built around, and it wins on every axis except setup time: Cheapest per generation, structurally. You pay each provider's list rate, full stop — no reseller margin, no credit fee. At studio volume (hundreds of images, dozens of clips a week) the difference is real money. Every knob of every model: exact inpaint masks (OpenAI), Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance Smart Length, native 4K rates — none of which any aggregator carries. The cost: ~5 minutes per provider console, each with billing enabled.
Which path should you pick? › 2. One OpenRouter key — pick this if you care about simplicity

The 2-minute setup, and since v1.0.8 it's a genuinely complete studio: images with Brut's own size/aspect menus (all four Nano Bananas, GPT Image 2), the video set (Kling 3.0 std/pro and O1, Veo 3.1/Fast/Lite with end frames, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5), every planning model, and Marcel — chat, ambient narration and acting, with Anthropic prompt caching passing through so long conversations cost the same as on a native key. A unique honesty bonus: OpenRouter reports the exact billed cost of every job, and Brut writes it straight onto your ledger. What you give up: GPT Image 2 sizing (quality knob only), Kling 4K and the Omni / Turbo / 2.6 tiers, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images, Smart Length, Gemini Omni Flash, exact inpaint masks (approximate ones work), and the upscalers. Prices are pass-through list rates for text and images; video carries a modest margin.
Which path should you pick? › 3. OpenRouter + fal.ai — pick this if you want aggregator simplicity at better video rates

Two keys instead of one, and the route table quietly picks the better door per model: OpenRouter keeps text, Marcel, and images (its native-menu fidelity wins there); fal takes over video — its Kling rates run noticeably cheaper — and adds GPT Image 2 sizing via its own presets. This is the setup we'd suggest to most people who don't want provider consoles: one evening of video work typically pays for the second key's two minutes of setup.
Which path should you pick? › The pattern to remember

Keys you add later always take over their models automatically. Start with OpenRouter today, add fal when video volume grows, add native keys whenever one provider starts costing real money — nothing to reconfigure, the routes just step aside. Also supported, for narrower cases: a Higgsfield subscription (no key at all — Nano Banana 2 + Seedance billed to plan credits; no planning, no Marcel) and a Replicate token (a redundancy door covering roughly what fal covers, incl. Veo end frames). Both work, neither is where we'd start.

Silent content refusals. An image edit returning finishReason: OTHER (newer builds: IMAGE_OTHER) is a content refusal, usually caused by an input image (a real person's name in facade text, a face, a logo), not the prompt. Deterministic — Brut won't auto-retry. Remove or crop the offending image. Thinking tokens. Gemini 2.5+ text models spend "thinking" tokens from the output budget, and truncation isn't an error — just a cut-off with finishReason: MAX_TOKENS. Brut's planning layer checks for this and retries with more headroom, then fails loudly rather than silently.
Veo and Omni ride this key
