OpenAI provides GPT Image 2 and the GPT Image 2.5 pair (Flare and Sunburst, released 2026-09-08) for images, and GPT text models for planning.
Create a key at platform.openai.com/api-keys and paste it into ⚙ Settings → OpenAI. Like Gemini, image generation needs a billing-enabled account — a first-call 429 means billing, not a rate limit.

gpt-image-2 — text-to-image (/images/generations) and image-to-image (/images/edits). Set the aspect ratio and quality on the node. gpt-image-2.5-sunburst — the quality tier: higher image quality than GPT Image 2, stronger subject preservation, OpenAI's pick "where editing precision matters most". Same endpoints, same aspect and size knobs, and a longer quality menu: low · medium · high · xhigh · max. gpt-image-2.5-flare — the speed tier: a small model with image quality comparable to GPT Image 2, much faster. Same knobs and the same five-step quality menu. Use it to explore, then render the keeper on Sunburst. Both 2.5 models passed their first live runs on 2026-09-09, including native masked inpainting (Flare at 1K, Sunburst at 2K: only the painted region changed, cleanly). GPT Image 2 stays first in the menu and the default for new nodes (and for the Director's proof sheet) for now. Neither 2.5 model has an aggregator route yet: they need an OpenAI key.

GPT Image 2 is token-billed, so the real price depends on size × quality × aspect ratio. Brut ships a measured square-baseline table (from under a cent at 1K low up to ~$0.71 at 4K high) and shows the estimate before any paid run. GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst bill at the same token rates ($8/M image input, $30/M image output, per OpenAI's model pages) but the quality tiers are shifted: measured live, 2.5 max bills exactly what GPT Image 2 bills at high (1K $0.21 · 2K $0.43 · 4K $0.71), 2.5 high bills about GPT Image 2's medium (1K $0.054), and low / medium / xhigh sit around them (1K: $0.007 / $0.015 / $0.095). Same output for less, or better output for the same money, your pick. Flare and Sunburst bill identically at every tier, so Brut ships the same fully measured table for both. Things to know: Non-square is often much cheaper. OpenAI's token accounting can bill a 16:9 4K image at a fraction of a square 4K one (we've measured ~$0.15 vs ~$0.71 on GPT Image 2 at high quality; on 2.5, 16:9 high billed 0.50× / 0.40× / 0.57× the square price at 1K / 2K / 4K, and at 4K a 5:4 image billed 0.82×, 3:2 0.65×) — so treat the estimate as an upper ballpark when your aspect isn't square. Edits add a little on top. Measured on 2.5 at 1K high: an input image adds about $0.007 (a 20 MP render about $0.013), a second input about $0.009, an inpaint mask about $0.0035. The ledger holds the truth. Every run records the exact usage-priced amount OpenAI reported, never the estimate — check the spend panel for what a generation really billed. Text/planning — gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-5.5 for Refine and the cinema agents when you choose OpenAI as the planner. GPT-5.6 family — three text tiers with a reasoning dial: Sol ($4/M in · $20/M out — promotional through 2026-11-21, the deepest), Terra ($2/M in · $12/M out, balanced), Luna ($0.20/M in · $1.20/M out, cheap and fast — OpenAI cut it 80% in July 2026). Available everywhere text models are picked: Text → Text, the cinema agents, and Marcel's model lanes. GPT-6 Astra (released 2026-09-03) — OpenAI's frontier planner: 1M-token context, reasoning dial low → xhigh, $10/M in · $50/M out (long-context prompts bill more). Excellent for the hardest treatments and as a brain for Marcel's advice. One honest limit: Astra takes function tools only through OpenAI's Responses API, which Brut does not speak yet — so with your own OpenAI key Marcel can talk and advise on Astra but an acting turn stops before any call with a clear message. Via OpenRouter (switch the OpenAI provider off in Settings) his tools work on it today. A native Responses lane is on the roadmap.

GPT-5.6 models can think before answering, and Brut exposes the dial: none · low · medium · high · xhigh (leave it on default to let OpenAI pick). Higher settings give deeper answers and cost more — reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens, so an xhigh answer can spend several times the tokens of the visible text. The dial appears on the Text → Text node, on the Director (and the legacy crew agents), and — for Marcel's brain lane — in ⚙ Settings; always only when the selected model actually supports it. Changing it re-plans (cache miss), like any input change.

OpenAI is the provider that applies an Inpaint mask natively — a true masked edit, where only the painted region changes and the rest is pixel-faithful. (Gemini treats the mask as strong guidance instead.) If precise local edits matter, inpaint on OpenAI. The output is the input's size. Since 2026-09-09 Brut always sends OpenAI an explicit output size: with a mask, the input image's own dimensions (so a 2K render comes back at 2K, nothing resampled); without one, aspect auto means the input's aspect at the size tier you picked (1K / 2K / 4K). Before that, OpenAI's own auto let the model choose the output size — a 2048² inpaint came back at 1254², and edits of a 3500×5000 render came back around 1000×1600, on GPT Image 2 too. Explicit sizing also makes the cost estimate honest: every run lands on a table cell.

Brut sends no temperature to the GPT-5-class planning models. Truncation is handled loudly: a finish_reason: length triggers one retry with more headroom, then a clear failure — never a silently cut-off plan.

Kling (by Kuaishou) is Brut's most extensive video provider — a dozen image-to-video models, including the 3.0 line. There are two ways to pay for it: this page covers the REST API (credit packs); see Kling (subscription) for the cheaper plan-billed route.

Kling supports dual auth, and Brut accepts both: New style — an api-key-kling-… token, used as a plain Bearer token. Legacy — an AccessKey : SecretKey pair. Store it in Brut as ak:sk (Brut mints the JWT for you). Get credentials at app.klingai.com/global/dev and paste into ⚙ Settings → Kling. Heads up on billing: Kling API resource packs expire in 30 days with no rollover. For steady studio use, the subscription option is about 3× cheaper — keep the REST API for high QPS or Team needs.

Twelve image-to-video models (Kling 1.x through 3.0 Turbo). On the node you set duration, resolution, and — where the model supports it — audio and an end frame (Brut's engine-wide convention: the end frame is the second init image).

Default base is https://api-singapore.klingai.com; override with the BRUT_KLING_BASE environment variable for mainland China. Kling's own docs return HTTP 446 to automated fetchers, so some passthrough knobs (aspect_ratio, audio) are best confirmed by trying them — a wrong knob surfaces the provider's 4xx verbatim on the node.

The same Kling models, billed to your kling.ai subscription plan instead of API credit packs — measured at roughly 3× cheaper than the REST API, with no 30-day pack expiry. This is the recommended way to run Kling for steady studio work.
How it's authenticated (no key to paste)

There's no API key here. Auth is an OAuth session owned by Kling's official CLI — and setup is two buttons on the ⚙ Settings → Kling (subscription) card (or in the setup wizard): Install Kling CLI — one click. Brut fetches the official CLI (@klingai/cli-global, about 1 MB) straight from Kling's npm registry channel and runs it on the Node runtime that ships inside the Brut installer. Nothing else to install, no admin rights. Log in to Kling — your browser opens on kling.ai; sign in there. Tokens are stored by the CLI itself in ~/.kling/.credentials. Check login confirms the session any time, and Log out (shown while signed in) drops it — switch accounts by logging out, then logging back in with the other one. Finished generations stay on disk. If you run Brut from source instead of the installer, the classic route still works and takes precedence: npm i -g @klingai/cli-global, then kling login — a CLI already on your PATH is always used as-is. Brut talks to Kling through the CLI (an MCP client) and never keychains those tokens — the vault just reports a cli-oauth sentinel when the session file exists. The engine downloads the watermark-free master (result URLs expire in 24 h).

The subscription model ids differ from REST — kling-video-v2_5, …-v3_0, …-v3_0_omni, …-v3_0_turbo, …-v2_6, …-o1 — and cover both image-to-video and text-to-video. End frame (tail image): v2.5, v2.6 and 3.0. The omni family (o1, 3.0 Omni) and 3.0 Turbo have no end-frame input. Reference images: o1 and 3.0 Omni take up to 6 extra references besides the start frame — the Image → Video node grows a references inlet when you pick them.

Only v2.5 currently carries a measured price (15 credits / 5s / 720p, ~3× cheaper than API list). Other tiers show no estimate until measured — Brut never invents a price it hasn't confirmed. When this provider is selected on an Image → Video or Film Shots node, the node shows your live plan balance ("🎟 Plan balance: 5,786 credits · Pro") read from the CLI — refreshed after every run — and Film Shots repeats it in the paid-run confirmation, so you always know where your credits stand before and after a batch.
No Kling sign-in? The menu still works

If you pick a Kling (subscription) model without the CLI sign-in, Brut falls back to an aggregator you do hold: Kling v3 / v3 Turbo / v2.6 / o1 route through your OpenRouter or Higgsfield credential, visibly marked ⇄ runs via … on the node (the provider and model pickers say so before you pick). (o1 via OpenRouter takes 5 or 10 s at 720p, no reference images.) Models with no aggregator anywhere (v2.5, 3.0 Omni) say exactly that — they need the Kling sign-in or the REST key.

5 QPS, Personal workspace only, and tasks can't be cancelled provider-side. Each seat signs in once (the CLI session lives per-machine, per-user). For higher throughput or Team workspaces, use the REST API instead.
Google's Veo 3.1 video models, for both image-to-video and text-to-video.
The key: it rides your Gemini key

Veo uses the same Google key as Gemini by default — if you've added a Gemini key, Veo just works, no second key to enter. Brut reports the source as alias:gemini. You only add a dedicated Veo key (in ⚙ Settings → Google Veo) when you want to separate the billing from Gemini; a Veo-specific key wins over the alias if set.

Veo 3.1 in three tiers — veo-3.1-generate-preview, veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview, veo-3.1-lite-generate-preview. All do image-to-video (with an optional end frame — lastFrame) and text-to-video. Set duration and resolution on the node; the node shows a cost estimate before you run.

Veo submits a long-running operation and Brut polls it to completion, then downloads the clip. Field names have moved across preview releases, so Brut extracts the video URI tolerantly and reports parse issues loudly — including content-filter flags (raiMediaFiltered*). As a preview line, expect Google to occasionally shift a field name; Brut surfaces the raw error rather than hiding it.
Google's Gemini Omni Flash (gemini-omni-1.1-flash) is a fast natively-multimodal video model: picture and sound generated together, a clip in under a minute, about $1 per clip. Added 2026-08-28.
The key: it rides your Gemini key

Like Veo, Omni uses the same Google key as Gemini by default. If you've added a Gemini key, Omni just works; Brut reports the source as alias:gemini. Add a dedicated key in ⚙ Settings → Gemini Omni only to split the billing.

Image-to-video from a start frame, optionally with an end frame (the two-image interpolation), and text-to-video. 3 to 10 seconds, 16:9 or 9:16, output at 360p, 720p, 1080p or 4k. Note that 1080p and 4k are upscales of the 720p render, not a sharper generation; if you plan a Topaz pass anyway, generate at 720p. Reference images on the references inlet: extra images of a subject (a product, a character, a facade) the clip should stay faithful to. Name them in the prompt. Audio is always on. There is no switch; describe the sound you want, or say "no dialogue, no music, natural ambience only". Every clip carries Google's invisible SynthID watermark. No negative-prompt field exists on Omni: whatever you type in the node's negative prompt is folded into the prompt as "Avoid: …", which is Google's own advice. The Gemini Omni video prompt preset in Refine writes the flowing-prose prompt style Omni reads best.

Omni lives on Google's Interactions API, a different endpoint from both Gemini images and Veo. Brut submits the interaction in the background, polls it, then downloads the finished file through Google's Files API. The ledger row is priced from the token usage Google reports ($17.50 per million video tokens), so the spend readout shows the billed amount, not the estimate.
Pricing: flat per clip, so ask for 10 seconds

Google's page says "about $0.10 per second at 720p" (5,792 video tokens per second). What we measured on 2026-08-28 is that every clip is billed 57,920 video tokens — a 3-second 360p clip and an 8-second 720p clip cost exactly the same — which is the 10-second maximum × 5,792. So a generation is ≈ $1.01 whatever its length or resolution (360p/720p measured; 1080p/4k upscales not yet, the node shows $? there). The practical rule: ask for 10 seconds — the node defaults to it — and trim in the Sequence node if you want less. If Google's billing page shows you something different, tell us; the ledger keeps the raw token counts. Google keeps the interaction (your prompt, inputs and the clip) on its side for a while after it completes; that is what lets Omni edit its own earlier clips. Brut doesn't use that yet: editing and extending clips arrive with the Video → Video node after the September conference, together with the region note that matters for European users (Google doesn't allow editing or extending uploaded videos from the EEA, Switzerland or the UK; editing clips Omni generated itself is allowed).

Anthropic's Claude joins Brut as a planning model — text only. It generates no images or video; it's there to be your director: writing the concept, look and shot plan on the Director node, and powering the Refine node.
Create a key in the Anthropic Console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Anthropic (Claude). Brut validates it by listing models.

Anywhere Brut asks "which LLM should plan this?" — the Director (and the legacy crew agents), Text→Text and the Refine presets — you can pick Claude, Gemini or GPT. Claude reads your stills (multimodal, downscaled to fit the request cap; generation always uses full-resolution images) and returns the strict JSON plan the chain expects.

Claude Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 5 (Anthropic's deepest generally-available model, added 2026-08-23) carry two knobs Brut exposes wherever these models run — the Text→Text node, the cinema agents, and Marcel's brain lane: Reasoning effort (low → max): how deeply the model reasons before answering. Deeper = better on hard treatments, more output tokens billed. Claude's own default is high. Thinking switch (Marcel's brain, ⚙ Settings): Claude Sonnet 5 thinks adaptively by default, and those thinking tokens bill as output tokens — so if Marcel feels slow or a chat turn costs more than expected, switching thinking off is the lever: faster, cheaper, a little shallower. The switch needs your native Anthropic key (turns routed through an aggregator can't carry it — Brut refuses loudly rather than silently thinking anyway). Haiku 4.5 supports neither knob (it's the cheap narrator lane — that's fine).

Truncation is handled loudly: a stop_reason: max_tokens triggers one retry with more headroom, then a clear failure — never a silently cut-off plan. Because Claude is text-only, it never enters the paid generation queue — it's a cheap planning brain, not a renderer. For available model ids and pricing, see Anthropic's console; Brut's catalog lists the ones it exposes.
Seedance (BytePlus ModelArk) is ByteDance's video family with native audio: a clip comes with sound in one pass. Brut carries Seedance 2.5 (the current flagship, added 2026-08-28) and Seedance 2.0.

Create a ModelArk key in the BytePlus console and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Seedance (or set ARK_API_KEY). Pay-as-you-go needs an account balance above USD 30, or a resource pack for the model you'll run. Activate the model first. ModelArk models are switched on per account: open the model's page in the console (Model Square → Dreamina Seedance 2.5) and click Activate before the first call. Until then every request fails with "Your account … has not activated the model dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628"; Brut shows that message verbatim on the node.

Seedance 2.5 (dreamina-seedance-2-5-260628, first in the menu): Image-to-video from a start frame, or start + end frame, and text-to-video. 4 to 30 seconds in one clip, or smart length (the model picks). Long single takes are its headline. 480p, 720p, 1080p (1080p is 10-bit HEVC: it plays in VLC/mpv and modern browsers; older players may refuse it). Up to 30 reference images on the references inlet (a Reference Board plugs in). Address them in the prompt as @Image1, @Image2… in wiring order and say what each supplies ("@Image1 is the building, copy its materials exactly"). The clip's aspect ratio follows the start frame. Seedance 2.5 refuses a ratio on frame-to-video runs, so the node hides the aspect select and says so. Text-to-video keeps the full menu (16:9, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4, 21:9, 1:1). Native audio on by default (it costs nothing extra). Prompt grammar: integer-second beats (0-3s: …, 3-8s: …), () for music, <> for sound effects, {} for dialogue, "no BGM" / "no audio" when you want silence. The Seedance 2.5 video prompt preset in Refine writes this structure for you; Seedance 2.5 shot plan rewrites a whole cinema plan in it. Seedance 2.0 (dreamina-seedance-2-0-260128): 4 to 12 seconds, up to 4K, first/last frame, reference images, and it accepts an explicit aspect ratio on frame-to-video runs. Still the choice when you need 4K straight out of the model. Its grammar is different (shot labels rather than timestamps, full-width audio symbols): use the Seedance 2.0 video prompt and Seedance 2.0 shot plan presets for it. Both generations stay in the menu; pick per job. Watermark is always off. Video editing, extension and video/audio references exist on 2.5's API and come to Brut as a Video → Video node after the September conference. No BytePlus key? Both generations also run through an OpenRouter key, marked ⇄ runs via OpenRouter on the node. Seedance 2.5 there is 480p/720p only, 4 to 30 s, first and last frame, no reference images and no smart length, billed per video token at the same rate as BytePlus (the ledger records the exact billed amount). The 1080p tier and the 30-reference workflow need your own BytePlus key.

A start frame and references can't travel together. Seedance refuses a request that carries both an exact first_frame and reference images. When you wire references into Image → Video, Brut switches to Seedance's keyframe reference mode: the start (and end) frame ride as reference Image 1 (and 2) with "Image 1 is the first frame" in the prompt, references numbered after them. The framing is then approximate rather than pixel-exact and the clip's aspect is measured from the start frame. The node says so on its references line; wire no references to keep the exact first-frame behaviour. Photoreal faces are refused in reference images, generated or not. ModelArk's moderation blocks reference images or videos that look like they contain a real person, and it cannot tell an AI-generated face from a photograph (field-tested: a fully generated woman was refused as "may contain real person"). Only faces made by ModelArk's own models under your account, their preset digital characters, or authorized-person assets pass, none of which Brut carries yet. A populated archviz render can trip this too; crop people out of the references, keep them in the start frame only, or do character swaps on Gemini Omni or Kling Omni, whose gates accept generated people. Three concurrent tasks per individual account. Film Shots sends five at once; the extra ones queue on BytePlus's side and finish a little later, nothing fails. Output URLs live 24 hours on their side; Brut downloads every clip as soon as it's done.
Pricing, read this before you buy credits

Seedance's billing has two sharp edges: Credit packs are model-bound. A Seedance 2.5 pack does not cover 2.0 (or the fast/mini tiers), and vice versa. Buy the pack that matches the model you'll run, or use pay-as-you-go. Rates are per token, and tokens depend on resolution and on whether the request contains video. Tokens ≈ width × height × 24 × seconds ÷ 1024. Brut's catalog turns BytePlus's list rates into per-second estimates: Seedance 2.5 ~ per second (16:9, no video input) 480p $0.10 720p $0.23 1080p $0.57 list, $0.41 through 17 September 2026 (BytePlus launch promo, applied automatically until that date) Seedance 2.0 ~ per second 480p $0.07 720p $0.15 1080p $0.37 4K $0.78 The node shows the estimate before you run, and Film Shots itemizes it per clip. The ledger row is priced from BytePlus's own token count (the usage the API returns), not from the estimate, so what you see in the spend readout is what you were billed. Failed generations cost nothing.

Magnific is the reference AI image upscaler. Brut integrates its two upscaling endpoints — Upscaler Creative and Upscaler Precision V2 — in the Upscale Image node. Brut deliberately uses only the upscalers, not Magnific's other generation endpoints.

Generate an API key on your Magnific dashboard (API Keys page) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Magnific (or set MAGNIFIC_API_KEY). You do not need the webhook secret: Brut runs on your machine and polls Magnific for results directly — no webhooks, no third-party relay, nothing in the call path but you and Magnific.

The API bills credits from your Magnific subscription's allocation (for example, Premium+ includes 600K credits per year), consumed by output pixel area. Two things worth knowing: A credit's dollar value depends on your tier, so Brut doesn't pretend to convert: the ≈$ figure on the node is Magnific's own doc-derived pay-as-you-go equivalent — a rough ceiling, not what your plan actually charges you. On a yearly plan, your effective cost is simply your plan price spread over your usage; at studio volume upscales barely dent the allocation (a few hundred credits each against hundreds of thousands per year). "Unlimited" plans are unlimited in the web app only — API calls always consume credits. Brut would happily show your credit balance and per-run points instead — but Magnific's API exposes neither on individual plans (the analytics endpoints are reserved for team tiers, and task responses carry no credit field). If Magnific ships a balance endpoint, Brut will pick it up. Until then: your Magnific dashboard is the billing truth.

Brut sends the original file bytes — never a re-encode, never a downscale. If an image exceeds Creative's 25.3M-pixel input cap, the run fails with a clear message instead of quietly shrinking your work (use Precision V2, or crop deliberately). Upscales are async: they survive an engine restart and reattach, like video jobs — money spent is never output lost. Provider errors are surfaced verbatim on the node.

Topaz Labs powers the precision side of the Upscale Image node — the Gigapixel-class faithful upscalers (including a model tuned for renders and CGI) and the Wonder-class generative ones — plus the Upscale Video node (Proteus / Rhea / Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend). One key covers both. There are two ways to run Topaz video upscales in Brut: Topaz Labs (cloud) — the API below. Credits per job, works on any machine. Topaz Video AI (local) — if you own the Topaz Video desktop app and a capable GPU, Brut drives the app's own engine on your machine instead. No key, no credits, no cost per run — and the clip never leaves your computer. See local install below.
Create an API key on the Topaz developer portal and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Topaz Labs (or set TOPAZ_API_KEY).

Model Class When Gigapixel Standard 2 precision the everyday default Gigapixel High Fidelity 2 precision maximum source preservation Gigapixel Art & CGI precision archviz renders, illustrations, game assets Gigapixel Low Resolution 2 precision tiny sources, thumbnails Redefine generative photoreal invented detail, prompt + creativity dial Standard MAX generative true-to-input generative restoration Recover 3 generative damaged / heavily compressed sources Generative models cap input around 24–256 MP and cost more per pixel; the node fails loudly if your input × scale exceeds a model's cap — it never downscales your work silently.

Topaz bills credits by output megapixel: the standard class covers ~24 MP per credit, the generative class ~4 MP per credit, minimum one credit per job. Credits come from one-off packs or a subscription's monthly allowance — the per-credit price depends on how you buy (packs run roughly $0.195 down to $0.158 per credit; subscriptions less). Brut shows a pre-run estimate in credits (with an approximate $ at a representative rate), the node displays your live credit balance, and the spend ledger records the actual credits the API reports for each job. Your Topaz account page is the billing truth.

Async like every upscaler: jobs survive an engine restart and reattach — money spent is never output lost. Results are downloaded to your project immediately (Topaz keeps files 7 days, links 1 hour — Brut never relies on either). Provider errors surface verbatim on the node; "not enough credits" says exactly that.

If Topaz Video (or the older Topaz Video AI) is installed and licensed on your machine, the Upscale Video node offers a second provider: Topaz Video AI (local). It runs the same models — Proteus, Rhea, Gaia CG — through the app's own engine on your GPU. No key and no account — Brut auto-detects the install (⚙ Settings shows "installed · free"); the app's own sign-in covers command-line use. If you install it mid-session, hit Check install. Free — no credits, no confirm dialog; the ledger records the run at $0. Private — the clip is processed entirely on your machine; nothing is uploaded. Missing model weights download automatically on first use (a one-time pause per model). Output is HEVC (H.265) with the clip's audio kept, like the cloud path. One run at a time — a second local upscale queues behind the first (one GPU). Local jobs don't survive an engine restart (nothing was billed, just re-run). The non-standard install location can be pointed at with BRUT_TVAI_DIR (the folder holding Topaz's ffmpeg.exe) and BRUT_TVAI_MODEL_DIR (its models folder).

fal.ai is an aggregator — a usage-billed API that resells many generation models under one key. Brut uses it as a route, not a provider in its own right: it never adds a single model to the menu, it just serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key for them. If you keep exactly one key on this machine, a fal.ai key is the widest single door: it can serve the Nano Banana image family, GPT Image 2, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, and Veo 3.1 — each visibly marked ⇄ runs via fal.ai on the node whenever the route is active.

Create a key on the fal.ai dashboard (it's an id:secret string) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → fal.ai (or set FAL_KEY). fal has no free generation tier — add billing to the fal account before the first call, or the first run answers with a provider error (shown verbatim, as always).

Your direct key always wins. The moment you add a native key (Gemini, Kling, BytePlus, …), that model leaves the fal route and bills direct — usually cheaper. Routing is always visible. The node chip, the paid-run confirm, and the spend ledger all say "via fal.ai". Nothing routes silently. Honest prices only. Estimates for routed runs use fal's own list prices where pinned, and show none at all otherwise — never the native provider's numbers. Image routes are pinned from fal's model cards and cross-checked against real dashboard charges (Nano Banana $0.0398 — essentially the native rate; Nano Banana 2 $0.06–$0.16 by size; Pro $0.15/$0.30 at 4K; GPT Image 2 per size × quality, e.g. square_hd high $0.211, square low $0.0053 measured). Expect a margin over the direct API elsewhere (Seedance via fal is roughly 2× the native BytePlus rate; video rates unpinned).
What the routes can and can't do

A route carries exactly the knobs fal's endpoint declares — anything else fails loudly instead of being quietly dropped. Current limits worth knowing: Veo via fal takes no end frame — unwire it or add your Gemini/Veo key. Inpaint masks route APPROXIMATELY on the Nano Banana models — the same convention as Gemini native (the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee; verified live). GPT Image 2 masks don't route — exact masking needs your OpenAI key. GPT Image 2 uses fal's own size presets (square, landscape 4:3/16:9, portrait, auto) — the node's Size menu shows exactly those instead of Brut's aspect + 1K/2K/4K pair. No silent mapping: the menu is the contract. Nano Banana (original) renders 1K only via fal; pick 2K/4K models or add your Gemini key. Kling 3.0's 4K master tier isn't on fal — std/pro only. Audio on video models is always sent explicitly (fal defaults it ON and bills extra — Brut keeps your node toggle authoritative). Generations behave like every other async provider: downloaded to your project's disk, journaled, restart-safe, priced in the ledger.

Higgsfield is an aggregator with a twist: it's billed by subscription plan credits, not an API key — which makes it the door into Brut for people who hold a higgsfield.ai plan and nothing else. Brut uses it as a route: it never adds a model to the menu, it serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key for them, always visibly marked ⇄ runs via Higgsfield on the node. Current mirror set (verified against the official tool's own model catalog): Images — Nano Banana (image→image), Nano Banana 2 (text/image→image), Nano Banana 2 Lite (text→image, 1K), Nano Banana Pro (text/image→image, up to 4K), GPT Image 2 (text/image→image, sizes as Higgsfield's 1k/2k/4k resolutions). Video — Kling v3 (with end frames), Kling v3 Turbo, Kling v2.6, Veo 3.1, Veo 3.1 Fast, Veo 3.1 Lite (with end frames, 8-second clips), Seedance 2.0 — including the Kling (subscription) menu entries, so a seat without the Kling sign-in falls back here instead of dead-ending. Where Higgsfield lacks a knob the native API has, the node hides it and says so in the price note — the common ones: no inpaint masks, no end frame on Kling 2.6 / v3 Turbo / Veo 3.1 (non-Lite), and no audio switch on Veo 3.1 (clips come with audio).

Higgsfield has no API key. Auth is a browser sign-in owned by Higgsfield's official command-line tool, which Brut manages for you. In ⚙ Settings → Higgsfield (subscription) (or the setup wizard): Install Higgsfield CLI — Brut fetches the official tool from Higgsfield's own GitHub release (≈19 MB, one time, integrity-checked). Nothing else is needed — the tool is self-contained. Log in to Higgsfield — your browser opens on higgsfield.ai; sign in with your normal account. The session is stored by Higgsfield's tool on your machine — Brut never sees or stores the credential. That's it: routed models light up the moment the sign-in lands. A Log out button appears while you're signed in — use it to switch accounts (finished generations stay on disk). Higgsfield's own platform carries many more models (Kling, WAN, Sora 2, Veo, Flux, Seedream…). Brut adds a route only after verifying each one's real API contract against the official tool — the list here grows as they're pinned, never speculatively.

Generations bill your plan's credits, exactly as if you'd used higgsfield.ai directly. Brut adds nothing and shows no invented USD estimates — credit rates aren't pinned yet, so routed runs show no price rather than a made-up one. The ledger still records every run. Your direct key always wins: add a Gemini or BytePlus key later and those models switch back to direct billing automatically. Higgsfield resells other providers' models under its own margin — if you generate a lot, a direct API key is usually cheaper. The subscription route is about simplicity, not price.

A routed run carries exactly the knobs the route declares — anything else fails loudly instead of being silently dropped (Inpaint masks, for example, don't route). Audio on video models always follows your node toggle — never Higgsfield's default. Provider-side tasks may not be cancellable: cancelling in Brut stops the polling, but plan credits may still be spent. Outputs are downloaded to your project's disk like every provider — restart-safe, journaled, in the ledger.

Replicate is the third aggregator route in Brut — a plain API-token, pay-per-use service that resells official builds of many models. Like every route, it never adds a model to the menu: it serves models Brut already carries when you hold no native key (and no earlier route credential — fal.ai and Higgsfield are checked first), always visibly marked ⇄ runs via Replicate on the node. Current mirror set: Nano Banana Pro & 2 (text→image and image→image), GPT Image 2 (text→image and image→image), Kling 3.0 Omni, Veo 3.1 & 3.1 Fast (image→video and text→video), Seedance 2.0 (image→video and text→video).

Create a token at replicate.com/account/api-tokens (r8_…) and paste it into ⚙ Settings → Replicate (or set REPLICATE_API_TOKEN). Billing must be enabled on the Replicate account before the first run — errors come back verbatim, as always.

Your direct key always wins, and fal.ai / Higgsfield credentials outrank Replicate when present (catalog order). Replicate is the redundancy door. Routing is always visible — node chip, run confirm, spend ledger. No invented prices: image routes carry Replicate's own billing-table rates (Nano Banana 2 $0.067 · Pro $0.15/$0.30 at 4K · GPT Image 2 $0.012/$0.047/$0.128 by quality); video rates aren't pinned yet, so those runs show no estimate rather than a wrong one. The ledger records every run.
What this route can do that fal's can't

Veo end frames work (last_frame is a real input on Replicate's Veo 3.1). Seedance text→video is available. GPT Image 2 sizes ride Replicate's aspect menu — ratios plus explicit sizes like 2048x1152 up to 3840x2160; the node's Aspect select shows exactly that menu (the entries above 2560x1440 are marked experimental by the schema). Reference images ride on Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0, and Kling 3.0 Omni.
And its own limits (all fail loud, never silent)

Seedance tops out at 720p on Replicate — 1080p/4K need your BytePlus key. Smart Length isn't available either. Nano Banana 2 has no size knob — 1K only; pick Nano Banana Pro for 2K/4K. Kling 4K master tier doesn't exist on Replicate (std/pro only), and the Kling route is the Omni model. Inpaint masks route approximately on the Nano Banana models (the Gemini convention: the painted region is strong guidance, not a hard guarantee). GPT Image 2 masks don't route — exact masking needs your OpenAI key. Audio always follows your node toggle, never Replicate's default. Large input images (multi-MB keyframes) are uploaded through Replicate's Files API automatically; outputs are downloaded to your project's disk immediately — restart-safe, journaled, in the ledger.

OpenRouter is the one aggregator key that can hold almost the whole of Brut: every text model (planning and Marcel — chat, ambient narration, acting), the full Nano Banana image family (incl. Nano Banana 2 Lite, the starter graph's model), GPT Image 2, and the video models — Kling 3.0 and O1, Veo 3.1 / Fast / Lite, Seedance 2.0 and 2.5. Outside it: the upscalers (they aren't resold anywhere, by design), Gemini Omni Flash and the other Kling tiers (3.0 Omni / Turbo / 2.6 / 2.5 and older), which OpenRouter doesn't carry. Like every route, it adds no models to the menu and is always visible: routed nodes show ⇄ runs via OpenRouter, and Marcel's composer says so too. If you want the simplest possible seat: one OpenRouter key is a working studio. Native keys added later always take their models back automatically, usually at slightly better prices.

Every text model in Brut's catalog runs at pass-through provider list rates — the same per-token prices as the native APIs (OpenRouter's revenue is a ~5.5% fee when you buy credits, not a token markup). Vision-grounded planning works, the GPT-5.6 reasoning dial rides along, and Anthropic prompt caching passes through — Marcel's long system context caches exactly as on a native Anthropic key (write premiums and 0.1× reads verified live), so routed conversations cost the same as native ones.

The Nano Banana family runs with Brut's own menus — the real 512/1K/2K/4K sizes and the full aspect list, unlike fal's preset system — which is why OpenRouter sits first in those models' route order. Approximate inpaint masks work (the Gemini convention, verified live). Billing is pass-through per image (~$0.069 measured for Nano Banana 2 at 1K, essentially the native token price), and every image job records its exact billed amount on the ledger. Two OpenRouter-specific limits worth knowing: Requests cap at ~52 MB, and a full-resolution PNG render can eat that alone once base64-encoded. When an image stack wouldn't fit, Brut transcodes the largest PNG inputs to full-resolution JPEG (q95) for that request only — never downscaled, never touching your files, logged in the engine console. If even that can't fit, the run fails loudly; export the source smaller or use a native key. Heavy 4K image jobs can be slow. OpenRouter's image endpoint is synchronous, and its queue sometimes stalls on large 4K multi-image jobs (measured in the field: a 4K edit that takes ~55 s on a native Gemini key can exceed Brut's 570 s route timeout entirely — that's on their end, not yours). If you hit the timeout: retry, pick a smaller size, or use the native key — which is the first-class lane anyway and takes over automatically the moment it's configured. The one exception: GPT Image 2 via OpenRouter has no size or aspect control (quality only) — so for that model fal and Replicate outrank it. It still works ($0.005 measured at low quality), just without sizing.
Video — the whole set, with billing truth

Kling 3.0 (std/pro) and Kling O1 (5 or 10 s, 720p, $0.112/s — the REST and subscription O1 entries both route here), Veo 3.1 / Fast / Lite (OpenRouter is the first route Lite has ever had), Seedance 2.0 and Seedance 2.5 (480p/720p only, 4–30 s, first + last frame, no reference images there — the 30-reference and 1080p features need the BytePlus key) — image-to-video with end frames, text-to-video, reference images where the listing declares them. Per-second rates (2026-07-22): Kling std $0.084 / pro $0.112 (audio +$0.042–0.056), Veo 3.1 $0.20 (audio doubles it), Fast $0.08–0.10, Lite $0.03–0.05; Seedance bills per video token. Where a surcharge can't be estimated up front the node says so — and it matters less than usual here, because OpenRouter reports the exact billed cost on every job, which lands on the ledger row verbatim (a 4s Lite clip billed $0.12 = 4 × $0.03, verified live to the cent).
Create a key at openrouter.ai/keys (sk-or-…), buy a few dollars of credits, and paste it into ⚙ Settings → OpenRouter (or set OPENROUTER_API_KEY).

Your native key always wins. Add a Gemini/OpenAI/Kling/… key later and those models bill direct again automatically. A fal.ai key can also run text (fal resells the same router) — but fal's text lane takes no images and no reasoning dial, so OpenRouter outranks it when both keys exist. Marcel routes here and only here: his lanes stream, and OpenRouter is the one aggregator whose wire supports Brut's streaming + tool-call + prompt-cache contract. Kling's 4K master tier, Seedance's Smart Length, Seedance 2.5's 1080p and reference images aren't on OpenRouter; Kling O1 takes only 5 or 10 s there. For video, fal outranks OpenRouter when both keys exist (fal's Kling rates run cheaper). Missing knobs always fail loud, never silently. Every routed call — text, image, or video — lands in the spend ledger with provider-reported figures (token counts, cache activity, billed cost), marked "via openrouter".

Brut's most ambitious workflow: turn a handful of stills into a finished, cut sequence — planned by a crew of AI agents, shot on the video provider of your choice, and assembled locally with ffmpeg, for exactly the bill it showed you. Stills → a crew that plans the film → a storyboard you edit → clips shot behind a confirm gate → a sequence cut on your machine. You stay in control at every step.

Conform → Reference Board → Director (plan + proof sheet) → Storyboard (keyframes) → Film Shots → Clip Board → Sequence → Preview Every arrow is a wire. The Director passes a plan document (JSON on a text wire); the boards are where you review and curate. Don't build this by hand the first time: the whole chain ships as the Cinema Director template — File ▾ → Browse library… → Cinema Director. It arrives pre-wired with the field-proven defaults (invented-first reel brief, proof sheets on GPT Image 2, keyframes on Nano Banana Pro at 2K); you add stills, judge the proof, pick your video provider, and run. Let's walk what it does.

Start from your renders — an Image In node (or a Multi-Shot contact sheet you've curated). Run them through Conform to a single aspect ratio (video wants consistency), cropping each to keep the right part of the frame. Wire the conformed stills into a Reference Board. This makes the pool visible and numbered — and the tile number is the still number the crew will refer to. Reorder to taste; the numbers are the contract.

One Director node. It plays the whole crew in a single call — concept, look and executable shot plan from one model that holds every shot in its head at once, which is exactly what keeps a film varied: the arc is distributed across the shots, lenses and framing change shot to shot, and no still is milked twice in a row. Pick a Brief and a Style, set shots and runtime, choose how much human presence you want, and wire it straight into the Storyboard. Every clip also gets a one-line ambient sound note for video models that produce audio. Before spending on keyframes, render the Director's 🎬 proof sheet: one cheap image of the whole film as a numbered contact sheet, all frames in one grade. Select the frames that don't inspire you, ✎ Reinvent rewrites only those clips (everything else code-locked), re-render for cents, loop — then 📌 pin the sheet you validate. The pinned sheet rides into every keyframe generation as the composition and grade reference — what you approved is what gets produced. Pick the Director's LLM — Gemini, GPT or Claude — on your own key. The plan is editable text: tweak a line and it flows downstream. Don't read the raw JSON — the node's 📖 Review opens the plan as an actual document: edit it in place for free, or leave 💬 margin notes and let Revise apply them (details). The four-agent crew (Scenarist / Artistic Director / DoP / Script Supervisor) is legacy since 1.1.1: the Director demonstrably plans better films in one call, so the crew nodes are hidden from the node browser. Graphs that already use them keep loading and running exactly as before — details.
2 · The Director plans the film › Invented shots — the flourish

Your stills define the project's identity, not the shot list. The Director invents most compositions — a detail close-up, a reveal, subtle human presence, the pull-back ending — each anchored on the stills that carry its materials, with a written keyframe prompt already styled to the film's look. The rule never loosens, it moves one level: one clip = one keyframe. An invented shot's start frame is generated (image-to-image on its anchor stills — and the validated proof sheet — with the identity clause appended, conformed to the film's aspect) before any video runs. An invented shot is never quietly sent as text-to-video — without an approved keyframe it simply refuses to roll. Want the full reel behavior? The Director's "Invent every shot" switch makes the stills references only — no shot animates one directly, every start frame is generated. Off, the brief decides shot by shot.

The Storyboard turns the plan into shot cards: per-clip start/end frame swaps with thumbnails, editable and lockable prompts, add/reorder shots, and ✕ mutes a card (greyed, kept, ↺ to bring it back) rather than deleting it. Change a line here and only that shot re-renders. It emits concrete image paths, so the next node just needs the plan wire. Behind the scenes the planning models are told the stills are numbered 1..N (models naturally count images from 1) and Brut translates their answers back to the board's 0-based numbers before anything is stored — so the plan you see always matches the board's tiles. A plan written under the old numbering (a cached or hand-pasted one whose last number equals the number of stills) is still renumbered automatically and noted in the Activity panel; a genuinely wrong anchor still fails loudly on its card, and 📖 Review on the Director lets you rewrite a shot's anchors by hand. Invented shots arrive frameless. Each shows its keyframe prompt and a 🎨 Generate keyframe button — pick the image model, resolution and (on GPT Image) quality once at the top of the board (the pending count and per-frame price sit next to it and follow your picks; keyframes are cents, clips are dollars). Generated keyframes cache on their prompt + anchors (an unchanged card never re-pays), ↻ re-rolls a fresh take, 📌 pins one against later prompt edits, 🕘 opens the card's history — every take it ever generated, from the project ledger — so a re-roll never loses anything: pin any past keyframe back as the start frame, free. Wiring any image into the card's socket overrides everything. Prefer to ground an invented shot on a real still after all? Just pick one in its start selector. The film's aspect is your call. The board's aspect dropdown (default: whatever the DoP wrote) conforms every keyframe to the format you choose and stamps it into the emitted plan. Switching aspect later doesn't re-bill: the raw render is kept and simply re-cropped, free. Batch it. ▶ on the Storyboard (or the 🎨 Generate N button) renders every pending keyframe behind one itemized confirmation — shot list, per-frame price, total. The per-card 🎨 stays for surgical re-work. Declining isn't an error: the plan flows on and Film Shots simply blocks the frameless clips.
3 · The storyboard — your edit bay › End frames, on demand

A clip's end frame used to come only from your stills. Now every card's end selector offers three states: none, a still of the board, or 🎨 generate. Pick 🎨 and the card grows a second frame block to the right of the start frame — same image box, same in-socket and out-plug, same tools — for a generated end frame that continues the start frame: it is rendered image-to-image from that start frame (a still, a keyframe or a wired image) as the frame being continued, with a continuity clause and the identity clause appended, conformed to the film's aspect. Where the camera arrives is now yours to direct, for grounded and invented shots alike. The prompt for that destination is written by the crew: an end-frame writer embedded in the Storyboard sees the actual start frame image, the clip's shot plan (the move, the subject motion, the atmosphere), where that start frame came from, and the reference board — and drafts the frozen final frame of that one move. Because a reveal or a pull-back shows what lies outside the start frame, the writer also picks the reference stills that show what the move reveals (at most three): they ride along as grounded context — the start frame stays image 1, the stills are "the same place, use them for what enters the frame, never for composition" — so the destination is extrapolated from your real project, not invented. It borrows the LLM (and reasoning dial) of the crew node feeding the plan wire — the DoP's or Script Supervisor's brain — one planning call, cents, ledgered like the crew's. Nothing renders from a prompt you haven't seen: ✎ or 🎨 on the end block opens a review — the start frame beside the drafted prompt, editable in place, ✎ re-drafts, and the writer's still picks as toggleable thumbnails (tick more, untick any) — and Generate renders. Cancel keeps the text and renders nothing. ↻ re-rolls a rendered end frame, 📌 pins it (it then survives prompt edits and a re-rolled start frame — otherwise a new start honestly orphans its end, since the end continues it), 🕘 opens the card's end-frame history. Wiring any image into the end block's socket overrides everything, and the block's out-plug carries the resolved end frame wherever you want it. Every prompt a card owns has a plug, too, in a labeled plug bar at the card's bottom: prompt in / prompt out, 🎨 keyframe prompt on invented shots, ⇥ end prompt on armed cards — so any of them can feed a Refine or a Text Board, and you can read which is which. ▶ on the board covers end frames too: after the start keyframes, one review lists every armed card at once — drafts filled in, each editable — and one Generate renders them all. An armed end frame that isn't rendered yet blocks that clip in Film Shots, exactly like a missing start keyframe: it is never sent without it. And when the video model has no end-frame input (only some do — Kling 2.5+/3.0, Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.0 among them), the clip still runs from its start frame, but the Film Shots table says so on that row — never silently. Budget-wise, an end frame is a second keyframe on that card (cents) plus one text call. Look at your frames. Click any card's image to magnify it full-screen, then browse the whole board like a gallery with ← / → (arrows or the on-screen ‹ ›); Esc closes. And every card has an output plug on its right edge carrying that clip's resolved start frame — the generated keyframe, the wired image, or the grounded still — so you can route a frame anywhere: into an Upscale Image for a delivery-res still, a Compose, a Preview. A card whose keyframe is still pending delivers nothing (never a wrong frame). The card's prompt has its own plug too, on the bottom-right — the final clip prompt, overrides and wired prompts applied — so a line of the DoP's wording can be reused or refined anywhere (a Refine, a Text Board, another card's prompt socket). And any card image can simply be dragged onto the canvas: it lands as a ready-filled Image In — detach a keyframe as the frozen base of a new exploration, safe from later re-plans.

Wire the Storyboard into Film Shots. It prices every clip — model, duration, resolution, cost — and shows an itemized confirmation. Nothing generates until you approve the total; cancel a line and it updates. A tick box per row chooses what gets sent (untick = kept in the table, greyed, not sent — render a few, judge, then the rest). Cached and pinned clips cost $0. Then it fans out, staggered to respect rate limits, with per-clip re-roll / ✓✗ / pin.

The Clip Board plays every clip — keep the good, ✗ the misses, ↻ re-roll one. Route the keepers into a Sequence node, which assembles them into one mp4 with local ffmpeg — cuts or crossfades, clip audio kept, vertical reels stay vertical, free. Drop a Preview on the end. Want it in 4K? Route a hero clip (or the assembled film) through Upscale Video — Topaz Proteus or Gaia CG, audio kept, itemized confirm before any spend. The shipped Cinema Director template already ends with this finish-in-4K tail (provider unset — the money choice stays yours).

The Cinema Director template is the reusable starting point — and any tuned chain of yours (a Director with your house style and dials, a Storyboard with your keyframe model) can be selected and collapsed into a composite or saved as your own template: one library item, every film starts warm. Why it holds together: grounding is enforced in code, not prose — one clip to one keyframe (a still of yours, or a frame generated from your stills and the validated proof sheet), still indices reconciled automatically, invented shots blocked until their keyframe exists, an anti-shake stability clause on every clip. The plan you approve is the film you get.
How do I resize a node?

Hover it: a small ⌟ grip fades in at the node's bottom-right corner (the same mark a text box has, applied to the whole node). Drag it to set width and height together; it lights up while you drag and fades out when you leave. Every resizable node uses this one gesture, boards, Preview, the text nodes, stickies and stamps alike, and the size is saved with the graph. Nothing to select first, and no frame around the node.
How do I send one output to several nodes?

Either drag a second wire from the same output port (an output can feed any number of inputs), or split an existing wire where you are: Alt-click the wire and a small dot drops on it. Drag a new wire off the dot to another node, or onto empty canvas to pick one from the add menu, already wired. The dot is only a branch point: nothing re-runs or re-pays because of it, and deleting it heals the wire. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I move all the wires from one pin to another?

Alt-click the pin whose wires you want to move (every pin starts pulsing), then click the destination pin. Output to output (or input to input) moves every wire across and keeps their other ends; an input then an output makes that output feed the input instead. Esc cancels, Ctrl+Z undoes. Details in Nodes & graphs.
How do I turn the home screen off?

Untick Show this screen at launch at the bottom of the home screen. Brut then opens straight on the canvas; the house icon on the left rail (above Settings) and File ▾ → Home still open it whenever you want it. The choice is per machine.
Why does a graph card show results I don't see on the canvas?

The card shows what the graph's saved file (or its live canvas, when it has unsaved changes) holds: the most recent results of its most downstream nodes, up to five. Hover the cover to flip through them. If a node's result was never saved with the graph (a run that finished after the last Ctrl+S), the card shows the canvas' own results and marks the name with a •.
Why does Marcel say there is nothing to recap?

Because nothing happened. At Narrator level Marcel recaps a project by himself the moment it opens, and the recap lands in his panel (the badge on the rail's Marcel button counts what you haven't read). A second recap is only worth a call when the diary holds at least five events and something new (a run, an error, a planner thought) happened since the last one; otherwise the engine skips the call and says so. Run something, then open the panel again.

During the beta, yes. At launch, Brut itself will be a paid tool: we sell the orchestration (the canvas, the caching that never re-bills unchanged work, the ledgers, the catalog kept current as providers churn, Marcel), never the tokens. Expect tiers with different feature sets, probably a limited free tier to see how it looks and a short trial; the exact terms are announced before launch. What never changes: generation is paid to the providers directly, on your own keys, at their price. Brut takes no cut, ever.
Where do my API keys go?

Into your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). They're used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider, are never written into a graph, never sent to us, and never appear in a .brutpack.
Can I cap what a project spends?

Yes — File ▾ → Project budget… sets a per-project ceiling compared against the ledger. The toolbar readout shows $spent / $budget and changes color as you approach it; paid confirmations warn past the cap (or refuse, if you tick hard cap). It's a guardrail on estimates, not accounting — the ledger stays the source of truth.
Can I turn a key off without deleting it?

Yes — every configured provider in ⚙ Settings has an on/off switch. Off = the saved key (or CLI sign-in) is ignored everywhere: the provider reads as unconfigured, and models with aggregator routes fall back to them — so you can test an OpenRouter-only setup, or bench a native key, without re-pasting anything. One tick brings it back.
Does Brut see my prompts, images or renders?

No. Everything you make stays on your disk (or your NAS). Brut has no server in the generation path. The only thing that ever leaves your machine is a tiny sign-in heartbeat — version/OS/install-id, no content.
Why do I have to sign in?

Today, to count seats during the beta. At launch, your account is also how you'll activate your plan on a machine. It's required, but it never bricks you: once you've signed in, a 30-day offline grace keeps you working through flights and outages, and if the sign-in server is unreachable a "continue for now" option appears. One exception, by design: a seat revoked for a breach of the beta license (a shared installer, a resold seat) signs out on that machine and paid generations stop until an active seat signs in. Nothing on disk is touched — your projects, outputs and keys stay yours.
Can I share Brut with a colleague?

Not the installer, please. Every beta seat is personal — that's the one rule of the beta license you accept in the app. Ask them to register on getbrut.app; applications are reviewed and approved seats get their own download link.
Windows says "Windows protected your PC" when I run the installer.

Expected during the beta: the installer isn't code-signed yet (a paid certificate we'll buy when the beta proves out), so SmartScreen flags it as unrecognized. Click More info → Run anyway. The installer runs per-user, without admin rights.
Where is my work on disk?

Everything Brut makes — projects, outputs, library, account state — lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut as plain files (keys are the exception: OS keychain). The engine's log is at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs\engine.log. Uninstalling never touches this folder — your work survives uninstall and reinstall. For any single image or video, right-click its preview. The same menu appears on every picture Brut shows, outputs and imports alike, board tiles, the magnifier, history rows: Reveal in Explorer opens the containing folder with the file selected, Find in ledger shows the run that made the file (model, node, graph, prompt, parameters, cost, date) and can open that node's 🕘 history on the row, Copy file path copies where it lives, Copy image puts the pixels on the clipboard (a video gives its poster frame) to paste straight into Photoshop, a chat or a mail, Export JPG writes a full-resolution JPG (quality 92) and Export web JPG a 2048-pixel one (quality 85) into the project's outputs/exports folder, no dialog, and Explorer shows the file. A Sketchpad's preview also offers Export PSD (see the Sketchpad page). The right-click on an image never opens the ring menu: that is for empty canvas only. Reveal is the reliable way to locate a result, because outputs are written to whichever project was active when the generation ran. File ▾ → Save project as… later moves the files the canvas uses into the new project (with their history rows), so the new folder is complete; a file another graph in the old project also uses stays there as a copy, and anything you generated there that the canvas no longer references stays where it was.
What do the file names mean?

Every file Brut writes is named <project>_<graph>_<node>_<provider>_<model>_<date>_<job> — for example tournesol_facade-study_t2i-12_openai_GI25F_260923_a3f91c2e.png: the project, the graph, Text → Image node 12, made by OpenAI's GPT Image 2.5 Flare, on 23 Sept 2026, ledger job a3f91c2e…. The model codes (NB2, NBP, GI2, K30, SD25 …) are listed on the Projects page. Per-tile files say which tile (ms-4-s07, film-3-c02), files you drop in keep your own filename, and the free local tools name themselves (conform, layers, sketch, sequence). The last segment is the key: right-click → Find in ledger turns any file back into the run that made it. Files from before keep their old random names — renaming would break every cache and pin that references them. The full key, and how to set your own pattern per project, is on the Projects & the ledger page.

Grab the latest installer from getbrut.app/download (log in with your beta email — the page always serves the newest build) and run it over the old install — no uninstall needed. Projects, keys and sign-in all carry over (see the previous answer for why). There's no auto-update during the beta. You won't miss one, though: at every launch Brut compares the version you run with the latest installer (it rides the signed-in heartbeat, see Privacy). If yours is behind, one line under the toolbar says Brut x.y.z is available with a Download button to that page; Later hides it for that version. Same version, no line at all. Offline, no line either. To check which version you're on: File ▾ → About Brut, at the bottom of the menu.
The taskbar shows a blank document icon for Brut.

A bug in the installers from 1.0.95 to the first 1.1.2 builds: the shortcut they wrote carried a comment longer than Windows can read back, and the icon path stored after it came out garbled. The taskbar draws the icon of that shortcut, so it showed a blank page while the app itself was fine. Fixed in the 1.1.2 build re-uploaded on 2026-09-14: install it over your current one, it rewrites the Start Menu and desktop shortcuts and the window now declares its own icon. If you had pinned Brut to the taskbar before the fix, unpin it and pin it again once, the old pin kept a copy of the broken shortcut.
My first generation returned a 429. Why?

Almost always billing isn't enabled on that provider's key — free tiers have zero generation quota, so the first call fails. Enable billing in the provider's console. A first-call 429 is billing, not throttling.
An image edit came back blank / refused.

On Gemini, finishReason: OTHER (newer builds spell it IMAGE_OTHER) is a silent content refusal, usually triggered by an input image — a real person's name in facade lettering, a face, a logo — not the prompt. Remove or crop the offending image. Brut never auto-retries it (it's deterministic).
Do I ever pay twice for the same thing?
No. Every node hashes its inputs; unchanged work is served from cache for $0. See Never pay twice.
What does ▶ Run do exactly? Does it generate everything?

No. ▶ Run is reveal-then-ask. Pass one replays every cached, pinned and free step for $0 and marks the nodes whose inputs changed (or that never ran) with a needs a run badge, together with what they would bill. If nothing needs a run, that's it. Otherwise one dialog lists them with the estimate: Generate runs the graph (cached steps still replay free; Film Shots, Upscale Video and the Storyboard keyframes still show their own itemized confirm first), Keep cached only leaves the badges on so you can see which nodes are outdated. The ▶ on a node runs that node and its upstream directly.
I reopened a graph and some results are missing.

Every generation node now shows its last result the moment the graph opens; the badge says whether it is current. If a node face is empty, it never produced a result in this graph. Hit ▶ Run to replay the cache and see what, if anything, would need generating.
I changed the prompt and lost a result I liked. Is it gone?

No — nothing generated is ever discarded. Every paid node has a small 🕘 in its title bar, next to ▶: it opens that node's full history from the project ledger, every result it ever produced. Pin any of them and it becomes the node's output again, free, protected from later re-runs until you unpin (the button turns 📌). Multi-Shot tiles, Storyboard keyframes and Film Shots clips have the same 🕘 per tile. See Projects & the ledger.
How do I take an image out of a node to work on it separately?

Drag it. Grab the image on any node — a generation preview, a Multi-Shot or Shot Board tile, a Reference Board still, a Storyboard card frame — and drop it on empty canvas: a ready-filled Image In appears there, pointing at the same file (no re-upload). Drop it on an existing Image In to append instead. The detached copy is a frozen base: re-rolling or re-planning the source never touches it.
A shot failed with "Network error — connection dropped mid-request".

Your connection to the provider dropped while a request was in flight (Wi-Fi blip, VPN hop, a provider hiccup). Re-roll the failed items — cached siblings won't re-pay. One honest caveat, written in the message itself: a response lost mid-read may still have generated (and billed) on the provider side; check the provider's console if it matters.
Can two people share a project?

Yes — put the project on a NAS and each seat opens the same folder, or pass a .brutpack file (warm caches included). There's no cloud sync by design; collaboration is file/NAS exchange. On a shared NAS project the studio timeline is shared too — one diary everyone writes to, with each entry tagged by who was signed in.

The Marcel button opens your project's studio timeline — a chronological record of runs, results, planner reasoning and errors, saved with the project so it survives restarts and travels with a NAS share — and the chat with Marcel, Brut's built-in companion. He knows the whole model catalog (with real prices), every node, and these docs; he answers on your own text-model key and every call lands in your spend ledger. An Assist slider sets how present he is on his own — from Off (silent journal) through failure diagnosis and run commentary up to Partner-level 💡 suggestions. A header toggle switches between the full engineer view and a chat-only view. It all stays on your machine (see Marcel, the companion and Privacy).
What happens if I kill the engine mid-render?
Video jobs are journaled and reattached on the next engine launch — same job ids, one ledger row, correct price. Paid work survives restarts.
Will I lose my canvas if I close the app?

No — the canvas autosaves into the project folder moments after every change, along with which named graph it is. Relaunch (any mode, any machine on a NAS share) and you're back exactly where you were. A • next to the graph name means changes not yet saved to the named graph (Ctrl+S), and opening another graph over unsaved work asks first.
Which video provider should I use?

For steady Kling use, the subscription is ~3× cheaper than API packs. Veo and Gemini Omni ride your Gemini key; Omni is the fast lane (a 10-second clip with sound in under a minute, flat ≈$1 per clip whatever the length — so ask for 10 s). Seedance 2.5 does native audio and single takes up to 30 seconds. All quote the cost before you spend.
What does "⇄ runs via …" on a node mean?

You picked a model whose native provider has no key on this machine, but you hold a credential for an aggregator that resells the same model — so Brut routes the run there, on your account. Your direct key always wins when present (it's usually cheaper); routing only fills the gap, it's always shown on the node and in the run confirm, and the ledger records it. Adding the native key switches the model back to direct billing immediately. Details: model routes.
How do I see my Kling plan credits?

Pick the Kling (subscription) provider on an Image → Video or Film Shots node — the node shows your live plan balance ("🎟 Plan balance: 5,040 credits · Pro") read from the Kling CLI, and Film Shots repeats it in the paid-run confirmation.
How do I report a bug or ask for a feature?
The green speech-bubble button on the left rail — see Install & first run. Diagnostics are opt-in and previewed byte-for-byte before sending.
Why does Brut ask about my session when I quit?

It's the beta asking for your experience while it's fresh: after a session that actually ran something (a Run click, a generation, or an error), the desktop app shows "Before you go" with a one-line summary and the feedback form. Nothing is sent unless you press Send & quit; Quit without sending closes the app at once. An empty session (open, look, close) never asks.

Brut is built local-first, and privacy isn't a policy bolted on afterward — it's the architecture. Here is, precisely, what stays on your machine and what (very little) leaves it.

Your prompts, images, renders and video. All of it is written to your disk (or your NAS), inside your project's outputs/ folder. Brut has no server in the generation path — your work is never uploaded to us, and we cannot see it. Your graphs and projects. Stored locally as files. A .brutpack or NAS share moves them between your machines; nothing routes through a cloud. Your API keys. Stored in your OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager). Used only for direct calls from your machine to each provider. Never written into a graph, never sent to us, never in a .brutpack. The engine log. The desktop app writes the engine's console output to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Brut\logs so problems can be diagnosed. It stays on your disk — a feedback report never includes it unless you attach it yourself. And the app never phones home for updates: the beta has no auto-update, so there's no update check leaving your machine either. Generation calls go from your machine straight to the provider (Google, OpenAI, Kling, Magnific, Topaz, …) on your key. Those providers see the requests you send them, under their own privacy terms — Brut is never in the middle. One provider-side detail worth knowing: Gemini Omni runs on Google's Interactions API, which keeps each interaction (prompt, input images, the generated clip) on Google's side for a while after it completes — that is the mechanism that lets the model edit its own earlier clips. Same key, same Google terms as Gemini and Veo. To be precise about that promise: there is no aggregator that Brut operates in the call path — no server of ours, ever. If you choose to run a model through a route (an aggregator you subscribe to yourself, when you hold no direct key), your requests go from your machine straight to that service, on your credential, under its privacy terms — and the node, the confirm dialog and the ledger always say so. One provider sends nothing at all: video upscales through Topaz Video AI (local) run entirely on your own GPU via the Topaz desktop app you installed — the clip never leaves your machine. One setup step downloads a tool rather than talking to a provider: clicking Install Kling CLI (for the Kling subscription provider) fetches Kling's official command-line client from the npm public registry — a one-time, user-initiated download of about 1 MB, integrity-checked, carrying no data of yours beyond the download request itself. Brut never auto-downloads anything.

Brut keeps a studio timeline per project — the running record of runs, results, and your conversations with Marcel, the built-in companion. It lives in a plain text file inside the project (ledger/activity.jsonl), on your disk or your NAS, and is never uploaded — it travels only where the project itself travels. When you export a project to a folder it's included by default (it's a backup); when you make a .brutpack to hand off, it's left out by default — a checkbox lets you decide either way each time. Chatting with Marcel works like every generation: the conversation goes from your machine straight to the text-model provider you picked (Google, OpenAI or Anthropic), on your own key, under that provider's terms. Brut is never in the middle, and every call is written to your local spend ledger with its token counts and cost. Images you attach to a chat message (the 📎 button) are sent to that same provider as part of that one message — never re-sent on later turns, and only files inside your project's outputs can be attached at all. When Marcel acts on your canvas, what he reads to do the job — your graph's structure, node prompts and parameters, output file names, journal search results — becomes part of that same conversation, so it reaches the text provider you picked, and nothing else. The actions themselves (placing nodes, wiring, running) happen entirely on your machine, and anything that would bill a key stops at an itemized confirm first. When Marcel speaks up on his own (the Assist slider at Reactive and above — failure diagnoses, run commentary, the recap when you open a project), the material he reasons over is the same local record: recent timeline lines, the error text, what's still running. That goes to your chosen text provider on your key, exactly like a chat message, and each remark is a ledgered call you can see. Set the slider to Off and nothing is ever sent unprompted. What Marcel remembers also stays on your disk. He keeps a taste profile — a plain-text note about how you like your images — tied to your account and stored beside your library. It is per-account, private, and never synced or exported: it does not travel in a folder export or a .brutpack. Project notes (a small memory for each project) live inside the project and travel with it, like the timeline. Both are plain text you can open and edit; Marcel proposes additions from your recent work and applies nothing to the profile until you approve it.
The local engine is locked to the app

Brut runs a small engine on your own machine (127.0.0.1). To make sure only the Brut app can drive it — and not some other web page you happen to have open in the same browser — the engine mints a secret token when it starts and requires it on every action that spends money or changes your files. The app receives that token automatically; nothing else on your machine can guess it, so nothing else can make Brut generate, delete, or spend on your behalf.
The only thing Brut ever sends

When you're signed in, the engine sends a small heartbeat — at startup and once a day — so we can count active seats during the beta. That's it. Here is the entire payload, verbatim: { "install_id": "a uuid minted once on this machine", "app_version": "…", "engine_version": "…", "os": "Windows", "os_version": "…", "arch": "…", "ts": "…", "eula_version": "the date of the beta license you accepted" } No content. No prompts, no images, no filenames, no graph data — ever. By construction: the code only ever assembles those eight fields. The license version you accepted. The date stamp of the beta license you clicked I accept on in the app — so we can show, if ever asked, that a seat took the terms. A date, nothing more. Nothing while signed out. If you're not signed in, no heartbeat is sent at all. The answer carries two things back: whether your beta seat is still active, and the version number of the latest installer. If a seat is revoked for a breach of the beta license, Brut signs you out and stops paid generations on that machine; your projects, outputs and keys stay exactly where they are. If the latest installer is newer than the one you run, a single line under the toolbar says so with a link to the download page; same version, no line. Nothing extra leaves your machine for that check: the version you run was already in the heartbeat. You can see this exact JSON any time in ⚙ Settings → Account.
Feedback — only what you type, only when you click send

The 💬 Send feedback button is the one other thing that can send data, and it's entirely user-initiated: nothing is ever sent until you press Send. A report carries your message, your account email (so we can reply), and — only if you leave the checkbox on — a diagnostics block: the same eight heartbeat fields plus the last few error messages from the Activity panel. The modal shows that block byte for byte before you send it ("Show exactly what will be sent"). Never your graphs, images, prompts or keys. The desktop app's quit-time prompt ("Before you go") is the same form under the same rule: it appears only after a session that actually ran something, and nothing leaves your machine unless you press Send & quit. Quit without sending is always one click.

Identity runs through Supabase (magic link or Google/GitHub). It's used only to know who's using a seat — never to store your work. The engine holds your session, not the browser: your refresh token is kept in your OS keychain, and access tokens are verified locally against a cached public key (so it works offline). This is identity only.

getbrut.app and this documentation load nothing from third parties — fonts are self-hosted, and there are no analytics scripts or trackers. Your keys, your work, your machine. The only thing we ever learn is that a version of Brut is running on some install, on some OS — and only while you're signed in.
